title: STEM Student Engagement with University Resources Builds Social Capital and Sense of Belonging: An Asset-Based Focus Group Study
abstract: Background. Attrition from STEM programs remains a persistent challenge for universities globally. To better support student success and socio-academic integration, universities have developed a range of curricular and co-curricular resources. Much emphasis has been placed on the benefits of these resources; however, less is known about how students recognize, access, and realize these benefits. Guided by a capital-mediated agency model, this asset-based focus group study examined how university-provided resources support undergraduate STEM students’ use of capital. We conducted four parallel focus groups with 21 students at a Norwegian university and analyzed narratives using thematic analysis. Results. Students described using both curricular and co-curricular resources to build personal/emotional, social, and human resource capital that helped them navigate academic and personal challenges. title: The Impact of the Erasmus+ Programme on Participation in Democratic Life, Common Values and Civic Engagement: A Study on Portuguese and Slovenian Adult Education Organisations
abstract: Active citizenship is one of the four main goals of adult education (AE) policy in the European Union (EU). While previous research has shown that EU AE policy has increasingly prioritised economic objectives, studies also suggest that Erasmus+ supports broader social goals. This study investigates how Erasmus+ in AE contributes to promoting active citizenship in Portugal and Slovenia. A mixed-methods design was employed, combining quantitative and qualitative data. Quantitative data were collected through a survey of 179 AE organisations, while qualitative data were obtained through document analysis, focus groups, and individual interviews with 17 representatives of AE organisations and 9 adult learners. The findings highlight the important role of Erasmus+ in supporting the social goals of European AE policy and suggest positive contributions to social inclusion, civic competences, critical thinking, and participation opportunities for adult learners, particularly among vulnerable groups. title: Developmental–Confirmatory Psychometric Evaluation of a Digital Peer-Assessment Microteaching Rubric Using Many-Facet Rasch Measurement
abstract: Digital peer-assessment systems can scale performance-based evaluation, but psychometric quality depends on how rubric criteria and rating categories function under rater-mediated use. This study used Many-Facet Rasch Measurement (MFRM) to evaluate and refine a microteaching rubric implemented in the Mobile Audience Response System (MOARS) and assess it in a subsequent cohort. In Cohort 1 (2024–2025; 27 preservice teachers, 331 peer rater–performance records), the baseline six-criterion, four-level rubric was examined through four MFRM specifications. The lowest category was used only five times, while the holistic overall-impression criterion showed comparatively low mean-square fit values and conceptual overlap with the analytic criteria. In this context, collapsing the two lowest categories and excluding the holistic criterion yielded a five-criterion, three-category analytical specification with ordered thresholds and performance separation of 2.98 (reliability = 0.90). title: Longitudinal Associations Between Homework and Examination Performance in Engineering Mathematics
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has renewed questions about whether take-home homework remains associated with performance on supervised assessments. This retrospective longitudinal study analyzed 759 student records from 15 cohorts of an engineering mathematics course (2009–2025). Annual Pearson correlations between homework and quiz, midterm-examination, and final-examination scores were calculated with 95% confidence intervals and pooled within three periods using inverse-variance-weighted Fisher transformations. Course-grade outcomes were treated separately because they could incorporate homework. Homework was positively associated with all three supervised outcomes in every cohort, although effect sizes varied across years. Pooled homework–final-examination correlations were 0.75 before COVID-19, 0.68 during 2020–2022, and 0.78 during 2023–2025. title: Preservice Early Childhood Teachers’ AI Literacy and Self-Efficacy in a Structured “Vibe Coding” Design Task: An Exploratory Pre–Post Study
abstract: This exploratory study examined a structured Vibe Coding task in preservice early childhood teacher education and its association with self-reported AI literacy, self-efficacy, attitudes toward AI, and technology acceptance. Vibe Coding was used in a qualified sense: participants created educational applications through natural-language prompting, then reviewed and revised the outputs. The task was implemented in two undergraduate courses using a convergent mixed-methods, single-group pre–post design without a comparison group. Quantitative analysis included 32 matched cases, while qualitative analysis drew on 26 reflective logbooks. All 32 participants also completed a researcher-designed, non-validated self-assessment rubric, reported descriptively. Paired-samples t-tests showed significant pre–post increases across all six self-report scales after Holm–Bonferroni correction. Effect sizes were large for AI literacy, self-efficacy, attitudes, and perceived ease of use, and moderate for perceived usefulness and behavioural intention. title: Student Motivation in Remote Laboratories: A Multi-Institution Self-Determination Theory Study in Food Science Education
abstract: Remote laboratories (RL) have expanded access to food science laboratory education while shifting students into more autonomous learning environments. Self-Determination Theory (SDT) suggests that motivation in such settings depends on whether psychological needs, particularly competence, are satisfied as students navigate hands-on learning with reduced instructor presence. This cross-sectional, multi-institution study examined motivational profiles of food science students (n = 110) who completed take-home RL kits at six U.S. universities, using the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory. In a linear mixed model accounting for institutional clustering (n = 109), perceived competence, utility value, and effort investment were each uniquely and positively associated with interest; in the corresponding single-level model, the three constructs jointly accounted for 57% of the variance in interest. title: Reflective Practice in Arts-Based Learning: Teaching Adults with Intellectual Disabilities in Inclusive Higher Education
abstract: This paper explores the development and delivery of an inclusive higher education programme for adults with intellectual disabilities within an Irish university. The programme was developed between two academic departments within an Irish University, to provide this student cohort with access to university life, enabling them to study and graduate alongside their peers. Central to the study is a module in arts-based communication, which aims to support students’ expressive, emotional, and social engagement in learning. Adopting a reflective, practice-based approach, the paper draws on the experiences of an educator involved in teaching on the programme. Through critical reflection on teaching practice, the study examines how arts-based pedagogies can enhance communication, participation, and inclusive learning environments for students with intellectual disabilities. The findings highlight the transformative potential of arts-based learning in supporting not only skill development but also confidence, self-expression, and relational engagement. title: Who Gets to Belong? Inclusive School Leadership and the Professional Experience of Early Career Teachers
abstract: This study found that inclusive school leadership shaped early career teachers’ (ECTs’) professional belonging, but its influence depended on whether leaders’ relational intent was supported by the organisational conditions in which it was enacted. Inclusive leadership was understood as the relational and structural practices through which leaders foster voice, psychological safety, and equitable access to support. This study adopted an instrumental case study design, situated in an Australian primary school. Semi-structured interviews with five ECTs were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, from which four themes were identified. Relational signalling from the principal shaped whether ECTs felt safe to voice uncertainty. Leadership functioned as emotional co-regulation in demanding moments, though its sustainability varied. Organisational routines produced a hidden curriculum through which ECTs learned when belonging was conditional. In high-stakes situations, guided participation actively drew ECTs into professional community practices. abstract: Time-limited robotics assessments can misrepresent classroom performance when unfinished attempts are discarded or recorded as exact completion times. This exploratory study addresses a practical reporting need: describing immediate execution and post-task perceptions while retaining non-completion, rather than ranking educational technologies. Thirty-five novice lower-secondary students participated in an approximately 80 min challenge-based implementation in three intact cohorts (n=16, 11, and 8). title: Rethinking Technology-Driven Sustainability Education Through Intermediality: Cultural Mediation, Literary and Artistic Humanities, and the Sustainable Development Goals
abstract: The implementation of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) across educational contexts has generated substantial research on pedagogies aligned with technology-driven sustainability education. Recent scholarship increasingly recognises that sustainability transitions require not only technological innovation but also cultural transformations capable of reshaping social norms, environmental imaginaries, and collective values. However, the processes through which sustainability meanings are mediated across different cultural and media environments remain insufficiently explored. This article argues that intermediality provides a valuable analytical framework for understanding how sustainability knowledge is produced, transformed, and experienced through interactions among literary, visual, performative, audiovisual, and digital media. title: Ubuntu Translanguaging as a Decolonizing Pedagogical Framework: Reimagining Multilingual Literacy Education for SDG 4
abstract: This article advances Ubuntu translanguaging as a decolonizing pedagogical framework for multilingual literacy education, aligned with Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4). Drawing on Ubuntu philosophy and translanguaging theory, it conceptualizes Ubuntu translanguaging as a relational, asset-based framework that challenges linguistic hierarchies and affirms learners’ full linguistic resources. Grounded in Ghanaian educational contexts, the framework responds to deficit narratives that overlook the community-rooted pedagogies multilingual teachers already use, and shows how multilingual pedagogies strengthen comprehension, affirm identity, and expand equitable participation in education. Three questions guide the article: how Ubuntu translanguaging challenges colonial language hierarchies in curricula and policy, how it operationalizes SDG 4’s commitments to inclusion and equity, and how it can inform Global South–North research partnerships built on mutual growth. By centering indigenous epistemologies and positioning teachers as co-researchers and co-creators of knowledge, the framework offers a reciprocal model for achieving SDG 4.

title: Project-Based Learning in Girls’ Physical Education: An Exploratory Two-Cohort Pilot Study of Physical Activity and Motor Performance
abstract: Project-based learning (PBL) combines student-centred learning with motor practice, but evidence on physical activity and motor performance in school physical education remains limited. This exploratory pilot study compared PBL with teacher-led instruction in two non-randomised cohorts comprising 53 girls: 27 fifth-grade pupils in basketball and 26 seventh-grade pupils in aerobics. Each cohort included one intact class per condition. Outcomes included pre–post basketball motor tests, final aerobics performance and physical activity records from subsets of pupils. Motor comparisons were exploratory, and wearable outcomes were summarised descriptively at the class and lesson levels. The final aerobics score difference was −0.49 points on a 0–16 scale (95% CI: −3.75 to 2.78). title: Exploring Authentic Partnership in Distance Initial Teacher Education: Associate Teachers’ Perspectives from Aotearoa New Zealand
abstract: Partnership is widely treated as central to high-quality practicum in Initial Teacher Education, yet most research assumes local, ongoing relationships between Initial Teacher Education providers and schools. This study explores how Associate Teachers understand authentic partnership with a distance Initial Teacher Education provider in Aotearoa New Zealand, where placements are geographically dispersed, and partnerships are often short-term. Guided by an interpretivist qualitative design, the study drew on an online survey (n = 30), online focus groups (n = 7), and a live poll used as an elicitation tool (n = 7). Analysis identified four interrelated themes: communication as the foundation of partnership, clarity of roles and responsibilities, bridging theory and practice, and partnership and perceived support for Māori. The findings show that partnership in distance Initial Teacher Education is not best understood as either wholly relational or purely procedural. title: When a Six Does Not Appear: Prospective Primary Teachers’ Questions for Informal Statistical Inference
abstract: Teachers’ questions shape how students use data, representations, and uncertainty, yet little is known about the inferential opportunities embedded in questions formulated by prospective primary teachers using a provided representation. This study analyzed 133 questions produced by 45 prospective primary teachers for sixth-grade students in a semi-structured problem-posing task based on a dotplot of 60 die rolls in which no six appeared and two contrasting interpretations. Using theory-informed content analysis, we found that, under the scaffolded task conditions, most questions combined generalization beyond the observed data, data as evidence, and probabilistic language. Explicit comparison of the two interpretations was uncommon in the wording of individual questions, while future or unobserved outcomes and the data-generating process were more frequent foci. title: Improving Students’ Digital Literacy in School Education: Insights and Practices from Physical Education Teachers
abstract: The integration of digital technologies into all areas of life, including school education, is a global megatrend. However, researchers note a lack of research on students’ digital literacy within school curricula, and specifically, it has not been examined in the context of school physical education. To address this research gap, this study explores physical education teachers’ practices, experiences, and perceived challenges in improving students’ digital literacy. This qualitative study is based on 29 semi-structured interviews with Latvian school physical education teachers, and an analytical framework for students’ digital literacy consisting of eight core domains was used to analyse the data. The results reveal a broad range of teaching practices reflecting constructivist and natural or ‘no formal teaching’ approaches. In assessing students’ digital literacy, formative and summative approaches were identified. Addressing gaps and challenges in improving students’ digital literacy, the following domains of teacher support needs were identified: conceptual, practical, and technical. title: Literacies of Transnational Students of Color: A Critical Interpretive Synthesis Through an Intersectionally Informed Critical Race Theory Lens
abstract: Although racialization profoundly shapes global education, literacy scholarship concerning transnational students of Color (TSCs) frequently lacks an intersectional lens. This critical interpretive synthesis examines how existing studies conceptualize TSCs’ literacies and how their characterizations of race structurally and ideologically de/legitimize these practices. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we systematically identified, screened, and selected empirical studies, then conducted a critical interpretive synthesis using an intersectionally informed Critical Race Theory framework, reported in accordance with ENTREQ. The review protocol was retrospectively documented and registered on the Open Science Framework. From 1282 initially identified records, 121 studies met the inclusion criteria. Our synthesis indicates that most studies frame literacy as an ideological, translocal, and translinguistic social practice. title: Navigating Inclusive Practices in Supporting Neurodivergent Learners in South African Under-Resourced Mainstream Schools: Perspectives from School Principals
abstract: Principals in mainstream schools occupy a pivotal yet underexplored position in supporting neurodivergent learners within resource-constrained settings. Guided by the transformational leadership theory lens, this study examines how mainstream school principals navigate neurodiversity support in resource-constrained school settings. A qualitative descriptive design, rooted in the interpretivist paradigm, was adopted. Data were collected from eighteen mainstream school principals from the Johannesburg Central district, using a quasi-structured questionnaire. Four themes emerged: identification of neurodivergent learners; support structures and inclusive practices; human, material resource and systemic constraints; and principals’ policy recommendations and visions for inclusive education in mainstream schools. The findings reveal a significant gap between policy intent and school-level practice. title: Cultivating a Regional Geoscience Learning Ecosystem: Systemic Equity and Cultural Change in California’s Central Valley
abstract: The geosciences remain among the least racially diverse STEM fields, with limited progress over the past four decades. This article presents a case study of the San Joaquin Valley Geoscience Learning Ecosystem, a regional initiative designed to transform institutional culture and strengthen recruitment, engagement, and persistence for first-generation, low-income, and racially/ethnically diverse students in Geology and Environmental Science undergraduate majors at two Hispanic-Serving Institutions in California: Fresno State and the State Center Community College District. The project established a student cohort program, a faculty professional learning community, and community-based research experiences grounded in culturally-relevant pedagogy, place-based learning, and project-based learning. title: Variations in Equitable Sociocultural Interactions Across Learning Activities in Pre-K to Third-Grade Classrooms
abstract: This study used secondary data collected in public elementary schools from 2016 to 2019 to examine variations in equitable sociocultural interactions, measured by the Assessing Classroom Sociocultural Equity Scale (ACSES), among classroom formats (e.g., whole group, small group), content domains (e.g., language and literacy, math, science), and class sizes. The sample included 348 video recordings from 65 teachers. Results indicated that teachers made more connections to children’s home lives during language and literacy lessons compared to math lessons. Additionally, teachers provided children more Personalized Learning Opportunities during centers and small-group formats compared to whole-group formats. Analyses showed no variation in Inequitable Discipline or racially marginalized learners’ Participation and Engagement by content domain, classroom format, or class size. These findings point to the potential use of ACSES for measuring culturally responsive, equitable classroom management across multiple contents and classroom activity settings.

title: An Overview of Female Researchers: Demands, Job Resources, and Mental Health Among Brazilian University Faculty
abstract: Mental health problems among university faculty have been increasingly associated with intensified work demands, with women being particularly vulnerable due to persistent gender inequalities in academic careers. This study examined the perceptions of women faculty members at Brazilian public universities regarding work demands, organizational resources, and institutional practices aimed at promoting mental health and gender equity, using the Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) model as its theoretical framework. A qualitative study was conducted with eight women faculty members from public universities across different regions of Brazil, aged between 36 and 56 years (M = 46.5, SD = 7.05), most of whom were in stable relationships and reported household incomes ranging from BRL 15,000 to BRL 30,000 per month. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s Thematic Analysis. title: From Digital Integration to Digital Normalization: Generational Trends in Students’ Perception of Social Media Impact (2016–2022)
abstract: This study examines how students perceive the influence of social media on everyday life across a seven-year period (2016–2022), focusing on two domains: aesthetic–consumer choices and lifestyle-related orientations. The research uses a cross-sectional design with repeated annual cohorts (N = 589) from social sciences programs, applying a questionnaire adapted from an existing instrument measuring the perceived influence of social media on consumer choices and lifestyle-related orientations. Factor analysis revealed a stable two-factor structure, while trend analysis showed that both dimensions follow a gradual and moderate upward trajectory. The influence on lifestyle is consistently higher than on aesthetic–consumer decisions, which indicates that students interpret digital content primarily through everyday routines and values rather than market-driven cues. title: Automated Generation of Individualized Electrical Circuit Exercises Using Python and LTspice: Reducing Instructor Preparation Time
abstract: This study presents a methodology for the automatic generation of individualized electrical circuit exercise booklets using Python and LTspice and examines the academic outcomes observed after its implementation and its estimated effect on instructor preparation time. The methodology begins with the design of circuit theory exercises, which are subsequently parameterized and automatically simulated through Python scripts integrated with LTspice. Based on the simulation results, the system generates individualized exercise booklets, solution templates, and simulation files for each student while simultaneously collecting quantitative data to assess academic performance. The proposed approach enables both formative training and individualized assessment without substantially increasing the instructors’ workload. title: Developing a Professional Learning Framework for Alternatively Certified Teachers: A Delphi Study of Knowledge, Skills, and Dispositions
abstract: Teacher shortages and expanding alternative certification pathways have intensified the need for coherent support for teachers entering classrooms through nontraditional routes. This three-round Delphi study identified professional-learning priorities for newly alternatively certified teachers. Thirty-six K-12 teachers, administrators, and teacher educators in rural and semi-rural Montana completed all three rounds. Round 1 generated 120 open-ended responses, which were refined into 108 Round 2 statements; 97 statements advanced to Round 3. The study defined consensus as a mean of at least 4.00 and a standard deviation of no more than 0.75. The supplied final item lists contained 89 rated statements: 29 knowledge, 26 skills, and 34 dispositions. Item-level verification against the supplied Round 3 summary statistics showed that 53 of the 89 statements met both criteria: 7 knowledge, 19 skills, and 27 dispositions. abstract: Drawing on the Positive Development and Assessment Competencies (PDAC) model, this cross-sectional study examined whether character virtues and self-reported arts engagement make complementary contributions to primary school students’ self-perceived competencies. title: Exploring How Lecturers’ Behaviours Relate to Students’ Motivation to Participate in Self-Directed Learning in African Higher Education
abstract: Lecturer feedback, dialogical pedagogies, and supportive relationships are recognised as important for motivating participation in self-directed learning (SDL), yet the transferability of predominantly non-African evidence remains uncertain amid diverse African sociocultural, institutional, and resource conditions. This systematic review examined lecturer behaviours associated with African higher education students’ motivation to participate in SDL and challenges constraining lecturer practice. title: How Should School-Based Educational Digital Games Be Evaluated? A Proposed Framework for Examining Experiences Beyond Isolated Metrics
abstract: Educational digital games are increasingly incorporated into formal learning contexts. However, their evaluation often relies on isolated outcome measures that provide limited insight into how students experience, interpret, and assess gameplay. This conceptual article proposes a practice-informed critical-participatory framework for the student-centred evaluation of educational digital game experiences. The framework was developed through a practice-informed conceptual synthesis. This synthesis brought together recurring methodological concerns from school-based work and relevant scholarship on game-based learning, student participation, and mixed-methods evaluation. The framework comprises five guiding criteria: pedagogical alignment, learner and contextual suitability, multidimensionality, student participation, and triangulation. title: Differentiated Instruction and Learning Outcomes in Vocational Pharmacy Education: A Quasi-Experimental Study
abstract: Differentiated instruction has been proposed as an effective approach for addressing learner diversity and enhancing learning outcomes. The present study investigated the effects of a differentiated instructional intervention, informed by principles of cognitive psychology, Cognitive Load Theory, and educational neuroscience, on cognitive performance, learning engagement, and perceived cognitive load among vocational education students. A quasi-experimental design was implemented with 57 students enrolled in the Pharmacy Assistant specialty program of the Greek Public Employment Service Vocational Education Schools (EPAS DYPA). Two first-year and two second-year classes participated in both traditional and differentiated instructional sessions. Cognitive performance, learning engagement, and cognitive load were assessed through quizzes, application exercises, questionnaires, and rating scales. title: Professional Development in Education: A Qualitative Study of Public School Teachers’ Perceptions of Meaningful Growth and Mandated Practice
abstract: The present study investigates the professional development (PD) experience of ten public school teachers in British Columbia. The teachers are regular participants in school and district-based professional development (PD) programs. The research seeks to investigate whether PD is experienced as a genuine investment in professional growth or as time and resources that are wasted. Research suggests that traditional models often fail to produce deep, lasting change in practice. By investigating the professional and personal insights of teachers across grade levels and disciplines, the study identifies common themes in what makes PD meaningful, effective, or ineffective. These insights not only contribute to the understanding of teacher development but also offer practical implications for designing PD into the future that is relevant, engaging, and responsive to the realities of contemporary classrooms. The study contributes to ongoing discussions about how PD can more effectively support teacher learning as a socially mediated and contextually grounded process, affirming the value of aligning PD design with teachers’ professional agency and situated experience.

title: AI and Constructivist Pedagogy in TVET: A Scoping Review of Integration Mechanisms, Competencies, and Implementation Challenges
abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) is reshaping instructional practices by enabling adaptive, learner-centered environments that support competency development. Reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement and PRISMA-ScR, this scoping review examines how AI-integrated constructivist pedagogy facilitates competency development in TVET contexts. Searches across six databases and a manual website search identified 11 studies published between 2016 and 2025, spanning multiple regions, TVET levels, and domains. Findings indicate that problem-based learning and project-based learning are the dominant constructivist approaches, supported by generative AI and intelligent tutoring systems. AI-enabled constructivist environments were associated with strengthened technical competencies and enhanced transferable competencies including critical thinking, collaboration, and career readiness. abstract: Vocational training, which is currently on the rise, is practical teaching that prepares students for the performance of a profession. VET students have specific characteristics that make research necessary. The objective of this study was to validate and apply a questionnaire on the general attitude towards study (E-1) to a sample of 502 VET students and to determine the implications of personal and sociodemographic variables in motivations towards learning. title: Understanding the Nature of Science (NOS): Insights from Pre-Service Teachers’ Engagement with Scientific Biographies
abstract: The comprehension of the nature of science (NOS) is increasingly recognised as a crucial element of science education, and many countries have incorporated NOS-related elements into their national curricula. This development underscores the need to adequately prepare teachers to possess a thorough understanding of the fundamental principles of NOS. This article explores pre-service teachers’ understanding of NOS when engaging with scientific biography. Using biographies is proposed as a pedagogical strategy for embedding NOS within the curriculum. Grounded in the consensus view of NOS, this study evaluates students’ conceptualisations by analysing interviews and student presentations of the scientists’ life stories. The findings reveal variations in the students’ awareness concerning general aspects of NOS. Some pre-service teachers demonstrate a more profound understanding of science, recognising its tentativeness, social dependence, and the influence of human factors. title: Self-Perceived Ethical Knowledge in AI-Enhanced Teacher Education: Adaptation and Validation of a Scale for Chinese Preservice Preschool Teachers
abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into early childhood education has led to ethical concerns regarding children’s privacy, fairness, and developmental appropriateness. While ethical knowledge is recognised as an important component of teachers’ professional knowledge, existing instruments such as the Technological Pedagogical Content Ethical Knowledge (TPCEK) framework were developed for preservice teachers in general and do not fully capture the ethical issues specific to AI-supported preschool education. In this study, we adapted and validated a Self-Perceived Ethical Knowledge Scale for Chinese preservice preschool teachers based on the eight ethics-related dimensions of TPCEK. A two-phase sequential design was employed. In Phase 1, a three-round modified Delphi study was conducted, involving 20 experts who refined an initial 40-item pool into a 33-item scale. In Phase 2, we examined the scale’s psychometric properties by performing an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) on a pilot sample (n = 289)—with factor retention corroborated by principal-axis parallel analysis—and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) on a separate main-study sample (n = 583). title: Benchmarking Observable Platform Dynamics Beyond Persistence in Three Open Educational Datasets
abstract: Educational theories of artificial intelligence (AI)-supported learning include mechanisms absent from reusable platform logs. We separated a conceptual framework from four source-derived proxies: cumulative achievement, engagement, resource breadth, and digital activity. The Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD) was primary; Eedi provided external evaluation and EdNet an exploratory transport stress test, with 72,277, 7149, and 513 lagged transitions. In the OULAD temporal holdout, observable-state ridge regression reduced root-mean-square error (RMSE) versus persistence by 14.51–15.59% for behavioral proxies but by 0.16% for achievement. Autoregression captured 98.24–99.78% of behavioral gains; cross-state predictors added 0.038–0.324% beyond autoregression. Three outcomes supported prediction beyond persistence; none supported incremental cross-state prediction or coefficient interpretation. Same-feature gradient boosting improved behavioral-proxy prediction by 0.84–2.84% but worsened achievement by 3.47%. title: A Study on Improving the Usability of an AI-Based Learning Tool to Support English Diary Writing for EFL Students
abstract: AI-based writing support systems are increasingly being explored as tools for supporting English writing in educational contexts. In English as a Foreign Language (EFL) settings, learners often need support in generating ideas, organizing content, receiving feedback, and revising written texts. However, AI-based writing tools should be carefully designed and evaluated to ensure their usability, reliability, and educational relevance before being implemented in authentic learning contexts. This study aimed to design and evaluate the educational usability of WriteOn, an AI-based writing support system for EFL writing tasks that integrates AI and natural language processing technologies, including GPT-API, NLTK, spaCy, and BERT. Although the system was initially designed to support English diary writing in EFL contexts, its feedback structure and system architecture were intended to be extensible to broader writing tasks. A formative usability evaluation was conducted with eight experts in South Korea with backgrounds in EFL instruction, educational technology, instructional design, and human–computer interaction. title: Motivational Intensity, Enjoyment, and Shyness as Predictors of L2 Willingness to Communicate: Evidence from a South Asian Multilingual Context
abstract: This study investigated the intricate relationships among motivational intensity, foreign language enjoyment, boredom, shyness, and second-language (L2) willingness to communicate (WTC) in Pakistani university students. Using a quantitative cross-sectional de-sign, data were collected from 1050 English language learners via validated surveys. Partial Least-Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) was employed to test a moderated-mediation model examining how psychological variables influence L2 communication behavior. title: AI Writing Assistants in Higher Education: A Comprehensive Review of Impact, Literacy, and Policy
abstract: AI writing tools like ChatGPT, QuillBot, and Grammarly have reshaped university writing workflows. Controlled studies show gains in grammatical accuracy, student engagement, and self-efficacy, but none of the intervention studies retained in this review directly measured critical thinking or other higher-order outcomes, leaving concerns about overreliance largely untested rather than resolved. Synthesising 68 references published between 2008 and 2025, including 42 empirical studies, this narrative review examines how students utilise generative AI, its influence on core learning outcomes, and necessary institutional adaptations for policy and assessment. To address these shifts, the paper synthesises empirical findings across diverse study designs and proposes a seven-dimension AI literacy framework alongside practical design principles for effectively integrating AI tools into modern writing instruction.

title: Navigating Affective Cues in Video-Based Instruction: The Role of Instructor Emotions and Idiom Valence in English Idiom Acquisition
abstract: EFL vocabulary learning is an emotionally rich process, particularly in video-based instruction where learners encounter multiple affective cues. This mixed-methods study examined whether instructors’ emotional expressions and idiom valence influence EFL learners’ idiom acquisition and learning experience. A 3 × 3 within-subjects experimental design was adopted, manipulating instructor emotion (positive, neutral, and negative) and idiom valence (positive, neutral, and negative). Forty-five undergraduate EFL learners from a university in China participated in the study. After viewing each video, participants completed an immediate idiom recall test, a perceived learning experience scale, the self-assessment Manikin scale, a cognitive load scale and an open-ended questionnaire. The results showed that neither instructor emotion nor idiom valence had a significant main effect on immediate idiom recall. However, a significant interaction effect was observed, although follow-up comparisons did not identify a robust advantage for any specific congruent or incongruent condition. These findings provide implications for the emotional design of instructional videos in EFL vocabulary learning

title: Sources of Science Self-Efficacy in Primary and Secondary Students: A Systematic Review of Qualitative Research
abstract: Efficacy beliefs shape how students think about science and engage with learning. A substantial body of research has linked science self-efficacy (SSE) to outcomes such as persistence, interest, and achievement, prompting interest in how these beliefs are formed and sustained via Bandura’s four sources: mastery experiences, vicarious experiences, social persuasion, and physiological and affective states. Only six mixed-methods studies have examined how SSE develops using qualitative data alongside quantitative approaches. This systematic review examines what these qualitative contributions add to our understanding of SSE and what they indicate about the value of further qualitative research. The analysis identifies how students’ beliefs about their scientific capabilities are shaped through classroom interactions, teacher practices, assessment systems, and school cultures. Across studies, mastery experiences emerge as the most influential source, yet their impact depends on how performance, understanding, and progress are framed and interpreted. title: The Interplay Among L2 Grit, L2 Motivation and Self-Perceived English Proficiency: A Study on Myanmar Undergraduates
abstract: This study explored how Myanmar undergraduates’ language learning (L2) grit, L2 motivation, and self-assessed proficiency in English are related. The study was conducted in a Myanmar context, involving tertiary students from a public university. It consisted of two phases. The initial qualitative phase elicited data from eight participants, whereas the follow-up quantitative phase collected data from 336 students. Thematic analysis of focus group interviews revealed that the participants were gritty L2 learners, guided by intrinsic and extrinsic L2 motives. The quantitative results confirmed their high L2 grit and L2 motivation. title: Cross-Cultural Adaptation and Preliminary Validation of a STEM Attitudes Scale for Spanish-Speaking Children
abstract: This study presents the cross-cultural adaptation and preliminary validation of a STEM attitudes scale for Spanish-speaking primary-school students. A systematic review following PRISMA 2020 identified ten international instruments; a 27-item scale was selected for its comprehensive coverage of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics. The adaptation process followed international guidelines, including parallel translation, expert review, qualitative evaluation, and a pilot study with preliminary reliability analysis. Based on the results, two items were removed and the response survey was modified to an emoji-anchored Likert scale to reduce the cognitive load associated with abstract category interpretation and improve accessibility for young children. Psychometric analysis with 194 students in a Latin American context demonstrated excellent internal consistency (α = 0.952) and strong subscale reliability (α = 0.883–0.935). Exploratory factor analysis revealed a five-factor structure accounting for 66% of the variance: integrative STEM attitude, mathematics, science, technological application, and self-efficacy. title: Developing the Methodological Competence of Future IT Engineers in the Republic of Kazakhstan Through Problem-Oriented Learning
abstract: Kazakhstan’s transition toward Industry 4.0 and 5.0 increases demand for IT professionals capable of solving complex engineering problems. This study theoretically substantiated and empirically evaluated a didactic model for developing future IT engineers’ methodological competence through systemic problem-oriented learning. A quasi-experimental study involved 150 undergraduates from four Kazakhstani universities. In an integrated Smart Campus environment, students addressed authentic, industry-informed problems through an approach combining Challenge-Based Learning with the Four-Component Instructional Design model. Tasks included designing critical information infrastructure with provision for post-quantum cryptography and developing an intelligent energy-management system using fuzzy logic and the NSGA-III and MOEA/D algorithms. Performance on two engineering cases was independently evaluated using a 0–100 analytical rubric; scores were examined using the Shapiro–Wilk test, independent-samples Student’s t-tests, and Cohen’s d. The experimental group outperformed the control group in Case 1 (79.36 vs. 70.33; p = 0.003; d = 0.50) and Case 2 (80.61 vs. 71.12; p = 0.002; d = 0.53).

title: Patterns of Environmental Problem-Solving Among Lower Secondary Students in an Emancipatory Environmental Learning Project
abstract: Environmental problem-solving (EPS) is often assessed after instruction, limiting insight into how students demonstrate it during project work. This interpretive qualitative study examined EPS patterns among 35 Grade 8 students in a Thai secondary school during a 20-week project organized around the characteristics of an emancipatory approach. Three reflective journals provided primary evidence, while group worksheets and final presentations contextualized and corroborated students’ accounts. Hybrid deductive–inductive content analysis used five EPS components as initial codes while allowing patterns to emerge inductively. An end-of-project situational assessment provided complementary descriptive evidence without determining pattern assignment. Three overlapping patterns emerged: evidence-informed, action-oriented, and social change-oriented patterns. Students in the same course, and sometimes working on the same project, placed different recurring emphases on evidence, action, reflection, and participation. title: Tailoring Evidence-Based Mathematics Instruction: Developing Pre-Service Teachers’ Capacity to Support All Learners in Mathematics
abstract: Persistent concerns about the mathematics achievement of culturally and linguistically diverse students with mathematics difficulties have intensified in recent years, underscoring the need for effective instructional strategies to support this growing student population. Research suggests that culturally and linguistically responsive (CLR) practices can address these disparities; however, many teachers enter the profession without the knowledge or skills to implement CLR practices effectively. Preparing pre-service teachers to support diverse learners before entering the classroom is critical. Accordingly, this study examined the impact of a four-lesson online culturally and linguistically responsive mathematics instructional module (CLR-MI) on pre-service teachers’ knowledge, beliefs, and perceived ability to implement CLR mathematics instruction for students experiencing mathematics difficulties. The module incorporated evidence-based mathematics practices, culturally and linguistically responsive instructional strategies, classroom examples and non-examples, and interactive reflection activities. title: An Integrative Assessment Framework for Virtual and Augmented Reality in Educational Settings
abstract: The use of virtual and augmented reality (xR) in educational contexts opens up new pedagogical possibilities, but places high demands on planning, technology, and ethical responsibility. To date, no systematic tool is available to help educators and decision-makers evaluate use cases of immersive technologies in a structured manner. This article presents the EDU-xR Fit, an integrative evaluation framework that analyzes the use of xR scenarios across the core areas of pedagogical-didactic adaption and fields of action, as well as technical and contextual levels. The framework was developed through a multiphase exploratory design combining qualitative framework development with a supplementary quantitative persona-based weighting phase. The model also incorporates overarching factors such as appropriateness and ethical safeguards. In a web-based tool, key criteria are evaluated using a five-point Likert scale and linked to practical decision-making aids. The framework is proposed as a preliminary decision-support resource for educators and institutions involved in planning, assessing, and reflecting on xR applications. title: Digital–Relational Classroom Ecology: Teachers’ Perspectives on Digital Media, Self-Regulation, Reward Seeking, and Classroom Functioning
abstract: Digital media have become deeply embedded in children’s everyday lives, but teachers encounter their effects, or perceived effects, through classroom behavior rather than through screen-time measures alone. This study explored how 19 preschool and early-primary teachers in North Cyprus made sense of children’s digital-media-related experiences across four face-to-face interviews each, a structured follow-up, and a collaborative workshop. Interview material was examined through hybrid inductive–deductive qualitative content analysis. Teachers’ accounts converged around four areas: attention, stimulation, and self-regulation; relational and developmental functioning; external motivation, reward seeking, and attention seeking; and family–digital ecology. They also described uncertainty when similar classroom behaviors could be understood in developmental, environmental, or clinical terms. title: Research-Based Practices for Early Childhood Instruction on the Nature of Scientific Knowledge
abstract: It has long been recommended that the nature of scientific knowledge (NOS) be incorporated into science lessons, but unfortunately, this is not yet the case. Many researchers recommend that NOS be embedded in science lessons as early as possible, as research has shown that, given appropriate instruction, young children can conceptualize ideas about NOS, which can serve as a building block toward scientific literacy. In this manuscript, we describe the importance of teaching NOS to young children and share research indicating which strategies have been successful in improving young children’s conceptions of it. Our research question is, “What are the best practices for teaching NOS in early childhood settings?”. We then share results from a systematic literature review using the PRISMA approach of current research in NOS (within the past fifteen years) and describe successful interventions, such as the importance of explicit reflection and the incorporation of ideas through literacy connections, scientific inquiry, and STEM integration. Conclusions for the best strategies for teaching various aspects of NOS are shared, and recommendations for instruction and future research are made

title: REWIND: Environmental Role-Playing and Student Engagement in Climate Change Education
abstract: Climate change education increasingly calls for experiential and participatory approaches capable of engaging students cognitively, emotionally, and behaviorally. This study examined REWIND, a three-hour itinerant urban role-playing intervention on climate change and sustainable resource use, using matched pre-test/post-test data from 153 upper-secondary students in Italy. Outcomes comprised psychological well-being, pro-environmental behaviors, low- and high-threshold environmental activism, and educational orientations; experience-specific enjoyment was necessarily assessed after participation. Students from technical/professional schools increased in pro-environmental behaviors and low-threshold activism, whereas changes were not generalized across outcomes or school tracks. Male students, who began with lower low-threshold activism, improved significantly; however, their post-test scores did not differ from female students in either unadjusted or baseline- and track-adjusted comparisons. title: Early Language Proficiencies in Both Spanish and English Predict Later Academic Achievement in English Language Arts and Mathematics of Latino Children of Immigrants
abstract: Given the growing linguistic diversity in U.S. schools, there is a need to better understand how early dual language abilities contribute to later academic achievement. This study investigates English and Spanish oral language proficiencies at kindergarten as predictors of academic performance in third, fourth, fifth, and sixth grades among second-generation Latino children of immigrants (N = 228). Children’s early English and Spanish abilities were directly assessed using the Woodcock Language Proficiency Battery–Revised, and achievement outcomes were obtained from state standardized exams (MCAS) administered in English for English Language Arts (ELA) and Mathematics. A series of multiple regression models controlling for poverty, gender, and maternal education documented that English proficiency at kindergarten predicted ELA and Math performance across all four grade levels. title: Digital Dependency and Academic Identity Among Postgraduate Students in the Era of Generative AI
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has become embedded in everyday university life, often faster than institutional guidance has developed. This qualitative hermeneutic phenomenological study examined how postgraduate students experienced the boundary between generative-AI assistance and digital dependency, and how these experiences related to academic identity. In-depth, semi-structured interviews were conducted with eleven postgraduate students (five males and six females) at a public university in Saudi Arabia, selected through maximum-variation purposive sampling. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and returned to participants for verification. Analysis followed Van Manen’s holistic, selective, and detailed approaches to phenomenological reflection. Two themes captured the experience: negotiating the boundary of digital dependency, and academic identity between agency and dependence. title: Mapping Multilingual Pedagogies for Young Learners: A Scoping Review of Theories, Practices, Benefits and Challenges in European Early Childhood and Early Primary Education
abstract: This scoping review maps multilingual education practices implemented in European Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) and early-primary settings for children primarily aged 3–7. Mixed-age ECEC samples extending below age 3 were also eligible when the participating group served children within the target range. Following PRISMA-ScR guidance, peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2025 and indexed in Scopus or Web of Science were examined. Fifteen studies met the inclusion criteria and were analysed in relation to their theoretical foundations, pedagogical practices, reported benefits, and challenges. The reported practices drew on diverse frameworks, including translanguaging and plurilingualism, pluralistic and language-awareness approaches, bilingual and CLIL education, emergent literacy, oral-language intervention, and home–ECEC collaboration. title: Graduate Hydrogeological Education: Analysis of Pedagogical Content Knowledge in Water and Earth Sciences
abstract: Hydrogeology is an important field in graduate programs in water and earth sciences due to its relevance for understanding and managing groundwater resources. However, although university faculty members generally possess strong scientific and technical expertise, they often have limited pedagogical preparation for teaching complex hydrogeological content. Therefore, the aim of this study was to analyze the importance that postgraduate faculty members in water and earth sciences from Central and North American countries attribute to the conceptual, procedural, and attitudinal components of Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK) in the teaching of groundwater dynamics, and to explore whether these perceptions differ according to pedagogical training, academic degree, and teaching experience. The study employed an exploratory, descriptive–comparative quantitative approach with a non-experimental cross-sectional design. The study included 41 faculty members recruited through non-probabilistic snowball sampling. title: Navigating the Storm: A Qualitative Study of School Principals’ Crisis Leadership Practices
abstract: This study explored the crisis leadership practices that school principals perceive as effective and examines how these practices align with an established crisis leadership model. Adopting a qualitative research design, the study is based on in-depth interviews with ten Israeli school principals, focusing on their experiences in managing crises. Data were analyzed using a deductive, directed content analysis approach, with the crisis leadership model serving as the primary coding framework, complemented by inductive coding to identify new themes emerged from participants’ accounts. The findings revealed that principals enacted all seven overarching leadership constructs—compassion and care, openness and communication, adaptiveness, decisiveness, resilience and courage, consultation and collaboration and empowerment—through a combination of common strategies and customized, context-specific practices. title: Mapping Consensus in Evidence-Informed Initial Teacher Education Core Curricula
abstract: A robust, evidence-informed knowledge base for initial teacher education (ITE) is essential for preparing prospective teachers. Although a growing body of research addresses the content of ITE curricula, there is little consensus on what constitutes the minimal agreed knowledge for ‘learning how to teach’. This study reports a comparative analysis of two published, evidence-informed core ITE curricula. Items appearing in both were compiled into the Minimal Agreed Knowledge Set (MAKS) and corroborated against two research literature: teacher-effectiveness research and cognitive/educational psychology. The MAKS comprises 52 knowledge elements, organised under eight instructional principles and one category of general statements on teaching and learning, and represents areas of convergence between two frameworks from a shared, evidence-informed policy tradition. It is intended as a tool for ITE providers to review and refine their own curricula, rather than as a prescriptive programme. Implications for curriculum development and directions for future research on MAKS are discussed.

title: Development and Validation of the Instrumental Musical Self-Concept Scale for High School Students
abstract: In the field of musical learning, self-concept has received increasing attention in recent years. However, previous research in Spain has largely focused on students enrolled in specialized professional and higher music education, while instrumental musical self-concept in compulsory secondary education remains underexplored. To address this gap, the present study developed an ad hoc scale specifically designed to assess instrumental musical self-concept among secondary school students. The final sample consisted of 980 students from 14 educational centers in Aragón and Navarra (Spain). The results provide evidence supporting the internal structure and internal consistency of the 16-item Instrumental Musical Self-Concept Scale for High School Students, organized into four theoretically interpretable factors. These findings contribute to the study of instrumental musical self-concept in Spanish secondary education and provide an instrument whose psychometric properties can be further examined in independent samples and through additional sources of validity evidence.

title: Cognitive Language-Learning Strategies, Perceived Risk, and ChatGPT Use Among Croatian University Students: An EFL-Focused Study
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into university students’ language-learning practices, yet less is known about how established cognitive language-learning strategies and perceived risk relate to students’ use of ChatGPT ‘(OpenAI, San Francisco, CA, USA; model/version not specified). This study examined cognitive language-learning strategies, perceived risk, general ChatGPT use, and translation-related ChatGPT use among university students in Croatia. The full sample comprised 307 students, of whom 284 were learning English as a foreign language and completed the EFL-specific measures. Data were collected using a paper-and-pencil questionnaire and analyzed using Spearman correlations, age-adjusted analysis, and ordinal logistic regression. Cognitive language learning strategies were not associated with either general or translation-related ChatGPT use. title: Students’ Generative AI Use in Studio-Based Design Education: Selective Use, Design Judgment, and Studio Context
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping studio-based design education, yet relatively little is known about how students decide when and how AI should support their design process. This study examined students’ use, adaptation, and perceptions of generative AI, with particular attention to task-specific use, contextual adaptation, and factors associated with AI-related decision-making. An online survey of 112 undergraduate and graduate design students combined structured questionnaire items with optional open-ended responses to examine AI use across studio tasks, project stages, and learning contexts. Students reported higher AI use for concept development, research, and written articulation than for visual refinement, technical documentation, and later stages of design development. Students also reported becoming more selective in their AI use as projects progressed, while instructor expectations, peer influence, and concern about negative judgment were associated with students’ AI-related decisions. title: Validation of a Questionnaire to Explore Artificial Intelligence Use Among Upper-Secondary and Higher Education Teachers
abstract: Research on generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education has shifted from students to teachers, yet available teacher instruments rest on technology acceptance models, professional knowledge frameworks, or AI literacy, and none articulates dispositional conditions, teaching activities, and contextual consequences within a single functional logic. This study extends to teachers an instrument previously validated with students and grounded in Functional Behavior Analysis and the Interbehavioral Model of Didactic Performance. Participants were 233 Mexican upper-secondary and higher education teachers (mean age 47.22 years, SD = 10.44). The study is strictly psychometric in scope: it reports initial reliability and internal structure evidence, not a profile of teacher practice. Reliability was estimated with Cronbach’s alpha and McDonald’s omega with bootstrap confidence intervals, and the number of components was determined through Horn’s parallel analysis. title: Attractiveness by Design and by Communication: A Desk-Based Analysis of Croatian Teacher Education Programmes
abstract: Teacher education increasingly competes for candidates, which makes programme attractiveness a question of alignment between what programmes signal publicly and what their curricula offer. This study examines that alignment in the 14 Croatian university programmes through which candidates holding a disciplinary qualification acquire pedagogical competences (the consecutive model). Using a comparative desk-based design, qualitative content analysis and structured comparison were applied to publicly available sources through two lenses: communicated attractiveness (how programmes publicly frame the teaching profession, the student experience, and the transparency of demands and support) and designed attractiveness (what the curricula and intended learning outcomes formally offer). Alignment between the two dimensions was classified into four patterns. title: Pedagogical Interventions That Support Self-Regulated Learning in Secondary School Students: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: Self-regulation of learning (SRL) is a key skill for secondary school students, placing them as active and conscious agents of their own learning. It enables learners to plan, monitor, and evaluate their progress, fostering autonomy and responsibility. Teachers play a crucial role by designing pedagogical interventions that guide and support students across different learning stages toward achieving personal goals. However, further research is needed to understand how different pedagogical strategies have been used to support SRL in secondary school contexts. This study conducted a systematic literature review using PRISMA with two goals: (1) to identify and describe teaching strategies in pedagogical interventions for SRL in secondary education, and (2) to analyze how these interventions support students’ self-regulation. From 12 selected papers, seven pedagogical approaches were identified. The findings highlight the diversity of pedagogical strategies, technologies and assessment practices and indicate the need for clearer methodological guidance, teacher preparation and future comparative research on SRL interventions.

title: Social Media Use and Academic Procrastination Among University Students: A Systematic Review of Empirical Studies
abstract: The widespread use of social media among university students has raised increasing concerns regarding its possible association with academic behaviors, including procrastination. This systematic review aimed to synthesize empirical evidence on the relationship between social media use and academic procrastination among university students. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic search was conducted in Web of Science, Scopus, PsycINFO, ERIC, and PubMed and was last updated in August 2026. Quantitative peer-reviewed empirical studies examining the association between social media use and academic procrastination in university populations were included. Twenty-nine articles comprising 30 study samples met the inclusion criteria. Overall, the evidence indicated a recurrent positive association between social media use and academic procrastination, although the magnitude and form of the relationship varied across distinct operationalizations, including general use, problematic use, addiction, social media disorder, and platform- or behavior-specific forms of use. title: SDG 4 Through Relational Pedagogy: Latino Students’ Experiences of Belonging, Mentorship, and Inclusion
abstract: This article reinterprets findings from a previously completed qualitative bounded case study of seven Dominican, Puerto Rican, and Mexican college students from the Bronx through the framework of Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4). No new empirical data were collected for the present article. The original study examined how participants experienced meaningful teacher–student relationships across their educational journeys. Cultural-Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) serves as the principal interpretive framework, while familioso, used here as an emerging culturally grounded relational lens informed by familismo, helps illuminate family-like qualities of trust, belonging, mentorship, advocacy, mutual responsibility, and sustained support within educational relationships. The original study identified six themes concerning mentorship and identity development, relational learning communities, negotiated authority and authenticity, family-like relational structures, family cultural values, and cultural identity. title: Navigating Disruption: A Transformative Learning Theory Examination of Faculty Perceptions of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Academic Practices
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have rapidly entered higher education, challenging longstanding norms around authorship, assessment, and disciplinary expertise. While early GenAI scholarship has largely emphasized student outcomes, adoption trends, and academic integrity, comparatively little empirical work has examined how faculty and staff make sense of this disruption over time. Guided by Transformative Learning Theory (TLT) as an interpretive lens for faculty discourse, this qualitative study examines how educators interpret GenAI as a “disorienting dilemma” and how patterns in faculty discourse differ across two cross-sectional cohorts during the first year of widespread adoption. We analyzed open-ended survey responses to the question, “How do you think AI tools like ChatGPT will impact the future of your discipline?” collected at a large U.S. R1 Hispanic-serving public research university. Two cohorts were examined: an early-adoption dataset gathered in 2023 (n = 104) and a follow-up dataset collected in 2024 (n = 313). title: From Teacher Education to Middle Leadership: Developing Equity-Oriented Leadership in Primary Science Education
abstract: Equitable science education in primary schools depends on whether all pupils can participate meaningfully in the distinctive practices of science, including inquiry, practical investigation, observation, evidence-based discussion, fieldwork, and the use of specialist resources. Yet access to these experiences can be uneven, as primary teachers vary in confidence, subject knowledge, resources, and preparation for organising science-rich learning. While research has examined primary teachers’ preparedness to teach science, less attention has been given to how primary science middle leaders develop the capacity to support equitable science teaching and learning across their schools. This study explores how primary science middle leaders understand and enact equity-oriented leadership in relation to science curriculum, pedagogy, resources, assessment, and pupil participation. Using semi-structured interviews with fifteen primary science subject leaders working in English primary schools, data were analysed thematically to identify factors shaping science-specific leadership capacity. title: Does Shared Reading Promote Cognitive Development? A Literature Review
abstract: Shared reading is recognized as an educational method that promotes language development and emergent literacy during early childhood. However, growing evidence suggests that it influences additional developmental domains. This review examined empirical and theoretical literature with the aim of uncovering the potential of shared reading as an inclusive pedagogical approach for supporting children’s cognitive development by integrating findings on adult mediation, dialogic interaction, repeated reading, mental state discourse, instructional adaptations, and shared reading across diverse learner populations. The reviewed literature indicates that the effectiveness of shared reading depends primarily on the quality of the adult–child interaction. Adult mediation, instructional scaffolding, collaborative dialogue, and active child participation were found to be key instruments for supporting learning across home, preschool, and inclusive educational settings. title: Conceptualizing School Leaders as Organizers of Systems and Resources
abstract: This study examined distributed leadership at a school that underwent transformation over a ten-year period beginning in 2014. Building on theory, we focused on capacity building as a key construct in distributed leadership, connecting it to the vision for school transformation and to the distribution of responsibilities outside central administration. We explored how this vision was enacted within the mathematics department, aiming to understand how educators translate theoretical notions of distributed leadership into a site-specific vision at the department level. We developed a leadership model with three interlocking components: visioning and revisioning, building capacity, and exercising autonomy with accountability. Using four protocols, we conducted 27 interviews with 19 participants, analyzing to generate themes. Initial visioning encountered implementation tensions, prompting revisioning around four tenets. The vision of a less hierarchical decision-making process entailed creating a teacher leader position, whose responsibilities included leading curriculum development and instructional reform. title: Higher Education Institution Choice: A Systematic Review of Contemporary Trends and Decision Factors
abstract: Higher education institution (HEI) choice is increasingly influenced by digitalisation, internationalisation, intensified institutional competition, widening participation, and financial uncertainty. This study systematically reviews how institution choice has been conceptualised and examined across domestic and international contexts. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, 56 English-language, open-access studies indexed in Scopus were analysed through descriptive mapping and thematic synthesis, with the literature search last updated on 17 September 2026. The review examined publication and methodological patterns, geographical contexts, student populations, research directions, theoretical foundations and reported choice factors. The methodological profile comprised 23 qualitative, 22 quantitative, and eight mixed-methods studies among the 53 empirical publications. Within the selected corpus of 56 studies, the literature is geographically concentrated, while comparative studies are limited. title: Curriculum-Aligned AR for Secondary Physics: Learning and Engagement in Circular Motion and Magnetic Force
abstract: Static diagrams inherently flatten the dynamic, three-dimensional interplay of forces and motion, leaving secondary students reliant on imagination to grasp invisible vectors—a challenge consistently documented in high-stakes physics examinations. While augmented reality (AR) offers a promising medium to externalise these abstractions, rigorous classroom evidence comparing theory-driven, curriculum-aligned AR with standard instructional materials remains scarce. Grounded in Variation Theory, Cognitive Load Theory, and Constructivism, this study evaluated a smartphone-based AR application featuring seven 3-D models tightly mapped to the Hong Kong Diploma of Secondary Education (HKDSE) physics syllabus. Evaluating N = 171 Form 4 students (Grade 10 equivalent, aged 15–16) across nine classes in seven secondary schools, we employed a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test crossover design comparing AR against equivalent textbook images. title: Digital Skill Alignment over Time: The Dynamic Digital Skill Realisation Framework for Graduate Employability
abstract: Higher education is expected to develop digital capabilities that support graduate employability, but the labour-market relevance of those capabilities can change between acquisition and employment entry. This conceptual article develops the Dynamic Digital Skill Realisation Framework (DDSRF) to explain that transition as a time-sensitive process rather than a fixed skills match. A theory-building synthesis was constructed through targeted purposive searches spanning higher education, digital skills, graduate employability, labour-market alignment, skill decay and obsolescence, signalling, employer judgement, and unequal employment outcomes. The contribution lies not in introducing new individual constructs, but in integrating them into a temporally explicit process. The framework distinguishes capability formation from initial alignment, capability-side skill decay from demand-side obsolescence, and skill signalling from employer recognition and valuation. It further specifies how contextual conditions shape the conversion of recognised skill value into realised employability outcomes and how graduate outcomes can inform institutional renewal. title: Social–Emotional Competence Across Arab Educational Subsystems in Israel: A Comparative Analysis of Sector, Gender and SES
abstract: Social–emotional competence (SEC) is an important factor contributing to students’ academic success and psychological well-being. While research on SEC is widespread, studies within the unique demographic and ethnic context of the Arab minority in Israel remain scarce. This study examined SEC levels across three distinct educational subsystems (General Arab, Druze, and Bedouin), alongside gender and socioeconomic status (SES). A sample of 852 fifth- and sixth-grade students was recruited from 15 elementary schools in northern Israel. SEC was evaluated using an adapted 40-item self-report online questionnaire split into emotional and social subscales. A 3 × 2 factorial ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of the educational subsystem, with post hoc pairwise comparisons showing that Druze students scored significantly higher than both General Arab and Bedouin students. Intriguingly, independent t-tests revealed no significant differences in SEC based on gender, grade level or SES. title: Perceived Institutional Digital Education Conditions and Self-Reported Pedagogical Innovation at a Peruvian University
abstract: Digital education is now a core institutional condition of higher education, but technology access alone does not describe pedagogical practice. This study examines the association between perceived institutional digital education conditions and self-reported pedagogical innovation-related practice among 65 Business Administration faculty members at one private university in Huancayo, Peru. A quantitative cross-sectional survey used two study-specific 35-item Likert-type instruments. title: Teacher Wastage in Pakistan: How Education Systems Employ Teachers but Lose Instructional Capacity
abstract: Pakistan has expanded teacher recruitment across its public education system over the past decade, yet policy and monitoring reports continue to document substantial rural, school-level, and subject-specific teacher shortages. In this article, I extend the concept of educational wastage to teachers, shifting attention from the loss of teachers to the loss or underuse of instructional capacity among formally employed teachers. I identify three forms of teacher wastage. Pre-deployment wastage occurs when appointment does not result in classroom instruction because teachers cannot take up or sustain placements, political influence directs placements away from school staffing needs, or teachers recorded as employed do not teach. Structural wastage occurs when teachers in schools are diverted from or misaligned with instruction through transfer instability, non-academic duties, or subject or grade-level misassignment. Erosive wastage occurs when teachers remain employed but lack adequate pedagogical preparation, induction, mentoring, or continuing professional support. title: Discursive Legitimation and Operational Threshold of Gender in Initial Teacher Education in Chilean Physical Education
abstract: Gender perspective (GP) has gained increasing legitimacy in initial teacher education, although challenges remain regarding its translation into conceptually grounded practices. In Physical Education (PE), the issue is particularly relevant due to the persistence of a masculinized disciplinary tradition and the centrality of the body. This study analyses how, in the discourse of teacher educators from two Chilean PE programs, the importance attributed to GP and the declared actions to implement it are distributed. A descriptive qualitative study was conducted using quantitative-oriented content analysis of 40 semi-structured interviews, corresponding to the entire eligible teaching staff. A total of 184 statements were analysed with a deductive category system. Of these, 63.1% referred to the importance attributed to GP and 36.9% to declared actions. title: Effects of Predictive Reading Strategies on Reading Speed and Comprehension: Evidence from Non-English Major EFL Learners
abstract: The skill of reading effectively can be viewed as an important academic requirement. The investigation aims to explore the impact of predictive reading strategy instruction on the reading speed and reading comprehension of Computer Engineering students learning English as a Foreign Language (EFL).This study employed a quasi-experimental research method to conduct the investigation among 120 undergraduate EFL students in Shandong Province, China. The participants were divided into two groups, including an experimental group that received predictive reading strategy instruction and a control group that received conventional reading instruction for eight weeks. This study gathered data using three assessment tools, including a reading speed test, a reading comprehension test, and a Predictive Strategy Use Questionnaire. The researchers used descriptive statistics and Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) as the main statistical methods for the analysis. The results showed that predictive reading strategy instruction led to significant improvements in reading speed, reading comprehension, and predictive strategy use.
