title: Scenario-Based Learning for Teachers: A Multimethod Usability Study
abstract: Background: Teaching is a complex occupation that requires rapid decision-making across a variety of situations. Online, scenario-based professional development platforms can reach diverse users without facilitator support, making strong usability especially critical. However, formative evaluations of their usability and fit with teachers’ learning needs are rare. This study examines the usability of PRF4TeachersTM, an online scenario-based professional learning platform designed to support K-8 teachers to develop their instructional skills. Methods: Using a multimethod design, quantitative and qualitative data were collected in parallel and analyzed separately without integration. Participants were 18 female teachers (M = 8.24 yrs of experience, SD = 8.71), predominantly European American (61.1%) and teaching K-5th (66.7%) or 6–8th grade (33.3%). The System Usability Scale provided an overall index of teachers’ experience with the platform, while think-aloud and semi-structured interviews yielded component-specific feedback. title: Exploring University Students’ Experiences of Using Conversational Artificial Intelligence for Emotional and Relational Support in Experiences of Loneliness
abstract: University students’ loneliness has remained a persistent concern in the years following the COVID-19 pandemic and correlates with multiple mental health issues, yet little is known about how university students experiencing loneliness use conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) for emotional and relational support. This exploratory qualitative study addressed that gap by exploring how students in a UK university experiencing loneliness perceived their use of CAI for emotional and relational support, and how they positioned CAI alongside other coping strategies. title: Teacher Mental Health and Well-Being from the Pandemic to the Post-Pandemic Era: A Systematic Review of Interventions, Policies, and Persistent Gaps
abstract: Teachers’ mental health problems have remained persistently elevated since the pandemic, yet system-level responses remain structurally inadequate. This systematic review synthesizes 66 peer-reviewed studies and policy reports (2020–2026). Meta-analyses of 54 studies (256,896 teachers, 22 countries) found stress prevalence at 62.6%, anxiety at 36.3%, and depression at 59.9%. Longitudinal evidence shows no recovery across 2021–2026; teachers fare worse than comparable professionals on all well-being indicators. Interventions show moderate effects (g = 0.42; trim-and-fill-adjusted g = 0.34), but the latter is an exploratory sensitivity analysis suggesting small-study effects, not a precise publication-bias estimate. Out of 24 intervention studies, 91.7% target individual-level coping; no peer-reviewed quantitative study evaluates macro-structural reforms. We propose the Evidence Hierarchy Mismatch Theory (EHMT) as one plausible explanation, alongside competing explanations. title: When Nature-Based Activities Become Participatory: Pedagogical Mediation of Young Children’s Participation
abstract: Child participation is central to rights-based early childhood education, yet it is often interpreted as verbal expression, choice-making or general engagement. Nature-based activities may broaden young children’s participation because they offer sensory, material and spatial forms of expression. Their participatory quality, however, depends on pedagogical mediation. This qualitative study analysed 24 interviews with preschool teachers in Latvia to examine how nature-based activities were described as becoming participatory in early childhood education. Deductive–inductive codebook thematic analysis was guided by six participation dimensions: access to information, being listened to, expressing views, discussing relevant matters, influence on decisions and independent decision-making. Findings identified four linked pedagogical processes: making participation possible through sensory and material access to information; recognising participation in children’s non-verbal and multimodal expressions; making participation consequential by allowing children’s ideas to affect materials, time and activity direction; and supporting agency through scaffolded decision-making and manageable co

title: Game Development-Based Learning for Early Programming Education Using Scratch and the [ai] Explore! Game
abstract: This study examines programming achievement among Grade 4 students participating in a structured Game Development-Based Learning (GDBL) approach compared with students receiving traditional programming instruction. The intervention used a single coherent problem context derived from the [ai] explore! game to support the progressive introduction of programming concepts in Scratch. A total of 104 students aged 9–10 from five classes in a Croatian elementary school participated. Two classes were assigned to the experimental condition and three to the control condition. Students in the experimental group progressively developed a playable game over seven weeks, while the control group followed traditional programming instruction. An initial knowledge test was used to assess baseline programming knowledge, and a post-intervention assessment served as the primary outcome measure. Because the instructional condition was assigned at the class level, the primary analysis used an exact class-level randomization test. title: Curriculum Internationalization in Higher Education: Evolution, Fragmentation, and Emerging Critical Perspectives from a Systematic and Bibliometric Review
abstract: Curriculum internationalization has become a relevant field in higher education because it connects pedagogical design, intercultural learning, global competencies, and critical debates on knowledge production. However, the literature remains conceptually fragmented and unevenly represented across geopolitical contexts. This study conducted a systematic literature review combined with bibliometric analysis to examine the scientific configuration of research on curriculum internationalization. Following PRISMA guidelines, 160 publications indexed in the Web of Science and Scopus were analyzed using R packages, including bibliometrix, tidyverse, dplyr, and ggplot2. The analysis focused on scientific production, influential authors and works, collaboration networks, conceptual evolution, thematic organization, and emerging gaps. The findings reveal sustained growth in the field but also a strong concentration of citation-based influence among a limited group of authors and predominantly Anglophone countries. title: Cross-Cultural Adaptation and Validation of the Public Speaking Anxiety Scale (PSAS) for Portuguese Nursing Students
abstract: Public speaking anxiety (PSA) represents a significant challenge, with a notable impact on the development of technical-scientific and communication skills. Based on a quantitative, cross-sectional design, the present study aims to carry out the cross-cultural adaptation of the Portuguese version of the Public Speaking Anxiety Scale (PSAS), evaluating its psychometric properties and structural validity through confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). A convenience sample of 348 nursing students from a higher education institution in the Lisbon region was used. The PSAS is a multidimensional instrument composed of 17 items, which evaluates the cognitive, physiological, and behavioral components of the PSA. The adaptation process followed the robust translation method developed by a panel of experts, ensuring semantic equivalence and internal consistency (n = 10; Content Validity Index Global 0.95). The results indicate that the mean PSAS score is 48.02 ± 13.03 (range 20–33). title: Mathematics Education and Sustainability (2010–2025): A Mixed Bibliometric Mapping and Critical Curricular Analysis
abstract: This study examines research trends at the intersection of school mathematics education and education for sustainability during the period 2010–2025. Using a mixed bibliometric design based on 970 documents indexed in Scopus published in English, Spanish, and Portuguese, the study combined quantitative bibliometric mapping with complementary qualitative content analysis. The results reveal sustained growth in publications, organized primarily around STEM/STEAM approaches and technology-oriented educational frameworks. Keyword and collaboration networks show thematic diversification alongside a concentration of scientific production in Global North countries. Qualitative analysis suggests that sustainability is frequently incorporated as an applied or contextual dimension rather than as an integrated curricular component of school mathematics, although some emerging studies demonstrate deeper forms of socio-environmental integration. The findings highlight the need for research with greater geographical diversity, higher empirical rigor, and a deeper pedagogical approach.

title: The Role of Critical Reflection, Social Media Support, and Feedback on the Evaluation of True and False News Items
abstract: Learning to evaluate information in digital contexts relies not only on critical thinking but also on how children acquire and apply knowledge when evaluating news content. In an era in which children increasingly rely on social media as a primary source of information, understanding how cognitive and social factors shape judgments is crucial. The present study examined how an inoculation intervention, cognitive reflection skills, and social context (social media use and adult support) influence children’s credibility judgments of real and fake news. Children evaluated news items before and after completing an inoculation quiz with or without feedback. Results showed that feedback was associated with a greater difference in credibility ratings between true and false news items, but no causal effect of feedback on changes in these ratings. title: Teacher Support for Curriculum Adaptation and Inclusive Assessment in Rural South African Secondary Schools
abstract: Inclusive education depends on teachers’ capacity to adapt curriculum and assessment to accommodate diverse learner needs. However, teachers in rural South African schools continue to experience significant challenges arising from limited institutional support, inadequate professional development, and resource constraints. Despite policy commitments to inclusive education through White Paper 6, the Curriculum and Assessment Policy Statement (CAPS), and the Screening, Identification, Assessment, and Support (SIAS) policy, limited empirical attention has been given to the specific support teachers require to implement inclusive curriculum and assessment practices in rural secondary schools. This study explored the support that teachers require regarding curriculum and assessment to facilitate the implementation of inclusive education in rural secondary schools in the Sekhukhune District, Limpopo Province, South Africa. Guided by Vygotsky’s Sociocultural Theory, the study adopted an interpretivist paradigm and a qualitative case study design. title: Supporting Self-Regulated Learning in Primary Education: A Case Study in a Directed Independent Learning School
abstract: Supporting students’ self-regulated learning (SRL) in school is essential for fostering self-directed learners and depends largely on how teachers design learning environments and instructional tasks. The aim of this case study is to examine how SRL-supportive classroom practices manifest across two learning groups in a primary school implementing directed independent learning. Participants included 59 students from two multi-age learning groups and four teachers. Learning activities were observed over one school week in both groups, and teacher interviews were conducted before and after the observations. Data were analysed using qualitative deductive content analysis. Findings indicated that in both learning groups, SRL-supportive practices included supportive classroom structures, opportunities for student autonomy, scaffolding and co-regulation, and practices supporting a collaborative learning community. title: Technology-Mediated Scaffolding to Support Critical Thinking in Pre-Service Teachers’ Academic Writing
abstract: Developing critical thinking skills (CTS) is a central goal of higher education, yet pre-service teachers often receive little explicit guidance on how to apply them in academic or professional writing. This study reports the design, implementation, and initial examination of IDEA, a purpose-built platform for technology-mediated scaffolding in academic writing. The scaffold targets four CTS subskills: interpretation (clarifying meaning), analysis (examining relationships among ideas), explanation (articulating and justifying reasoning), and evaluation (judging claims against criteria). Using a design-based research (DBR) approach, 57 fourth-year pre-service language teachers at a highly selective Chilean university completed three structured writing tasks during one semester. The first two tasks were completed without IDEA; the third used the full scaffold. Students’ texts were assessed with an expert-reviewed analytical rubric. title: Pre-University Educational Pathways and Mathematical Literacy Among Prospective Elementary Teachers: A Multidimensional Analysis
abstract: This quantitative study examines the association between pre-university educational pathways and mathematical literacy among 227 first-year prospective elementary teachers at a Spanish university. Although experienced teacher educators are informally aware of this association, its relationship with specific dimensions of mathematical literacy has not been sufficiently investigated. Mathematical literacy was operationalized through processes and capabilities from the PISA 2012 framework and assessed using five released items. We combined descriptive and non-parametric group comparisons with principal component and cluster analyses, supported by qualitative inspection of written responses. Descriptive analyses indicated generally low and heterogeneous performance, whereas group comparisons suggest that the science and technology pathway is associated with higher performance across all processes and skills, and that social science students generally perform better than those who followed the humanities and other pathways. title: Implementation Characteristics, Students’ Perceptions, and Instructional Impact of Haptic-Enabled Learning Experiences in Higher Education: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: By enabling active hands-on exploration of structures and phenomena that are invisible or impractical to manipulate in real life, haptic technologies have the potential to enhance learning across multiple fields of higher education. However, a comprehensive understanding of their implementation, instructional impact, and students’ perceptions remains limited. This systematic review synthesizes evidence from 101 studies published between 2000 and April 2026 across 11 educational fields, extending previous reviews beyond their predominant focus on health sciences. The findings reveal that existing research is constrained by limited geographic diversity, small samples, predominantly quantitative designs, scarce longitudinal evidence, and heavy reliance on self-report measures. Only 24 studies explicitly grounded haptic-enabled instruction in theory, most commonly embodied cognition. title: The Compliance Trap and Relational Anchors in Structured Instructional Leadership
abstract: Instructional leadership is often displaced by compliance requirements, operational demands, and formal evaluation. This qualitative secondary analysis examined how teachers and principals described organizational pressures and relational practices during a 14-day Build Rapport, Inspire Feedback, Celebrate Success, and Exceed Results (BICE) leadership cycle across five Southern California public charter schools. Data included open-ended survey responses from 33 experienced teachers, interviews with nine teachers, and interviews with six principals. A role-by-source matrix and constant comparison were used to examine demands that displaced developmental work, valued leadership practices, and convergence or tension across participant groups. Two cross-cutting themes emerged. The compliance trap described how urgent operational and accountability demands displaced coaching, recognition, and relationship-building. title: Process-Oriented Assessment of Project-Based Learning in Analytical Chemistry: Tracking Students’ Experimental Decision-Making Pathways
abstract: Learning analytical chemistry requires not only mastery of analytical and calculation methods but also the ability to make consistent experimental decisions. This study tested a process-oriented assessment framework based on the experimental decision-making pathway (EDMP) construct and the analysis of student-specific decision-making trajectories. A quasi-experimental study involved 60 second-year students, 30 each in a project-based learning group and a control group with a traditional laboratory format. During an eight-week module on determining total iron in water, 2317 individual decisions were recorded; independence, justification, use of data, and revision patterns were coded for each event. Dynamics were analyzed using generalized linear mixed models and sequence analysis, and trajectory characteristics were compared with educational and analytical outcomes. In the experimental group, the proportion of independent decisions increased from 35.7 to 61.5%, and the proportion of data-driven decisions increased from 32.0 to 58.2%. title: Dissonance in Interactions with Parents: A Qualitative Study on Vulnerability and Trust and Implications for the Professional Development of Early Childhood Educators
abstract: The expectation of establishing an educational partnership with parents poses challenges for both parents and early childhood educators (ECEs). Structural conditions and diverging orientations often complicate cooperation between educators and parents. This exploratory qualitative interview study with 15 ECEs examines which situations in their interaction with parents they find challenging. Based on qualitative content analysis, tense situations in interactions with parents are interpreted through the lenses of vulnerability and dissonance theory. The results show that ECEs experience different dissonances, vulnerabilities, and varying forms of trust in their work with parents. While experienced ECEs report role-related tensions (dissonances), younger ECEs describe relational strains with parents. The findings highlight profession-specific challenges that are discussed in terms of their implications for ECEs’ (further) professional development.

title: Rural LGBTQ+ College Students in U.S. Higher Education: An Asset-Based Examination of Engaging Interactions and Institutional Environments
abstract: Rural LGBTQ+ college students remain understudied in higher education. This study provides one of the few large-scale, multi-institutional quantitative examinations of this student population. Using 2023–2025 National Survey of Student Engagement (NSSE) data from nearly 300,000 first-year and senior students across 872 four-year institutions in the U.S., we combined variable-centered regression analyses and person-centered cluster analyses to examine engaging interactions with others and engaging institutional environments. We found distinct patterns of engagement associated with rural background, LGBTQ+ identity, and their intersection. Rural students reported less frequent engagement in some interactions with others but generally had more positive perceptions of their environment. LGBTQ+ students, however, had more frequent engaging interactions with others but a less favorable view of their environment. The interaction between rural and LGBTQ+ identities was positive across all engagement outcomes. The person-centered analyses further emphasize the non-monolithic nature of rural LGBTQ+ experiences. title: An Exploration of the Self-Efficacy of Secondary School Pre- and In-Service Teachers to Teach Sustainable Food Literacy
abstract: Education is critical to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Sustainable food literacy provides a powerful context for transformative Education for Sustainable Development, enabling real-world learning in secondary schools. This exploratory cross-sectional study used the Norwegian Teacher Self-Efficacy Scale to examine the perceived self-efficacy of home economics pre- and in-service teachers (N = 173) to teach sustainable food literacy, administered via a global digital survey. Through content analysis and parametric and non-parametric descriptive and inferential statistical analyses, the study reveals that teachers’ familiarity with the SDGs intersects with their willingness to integrate them into teaching. Self-efficacy for teaching sustainable food literacy was generally moderate to high, with lower levels among pre-service teachers. Teachers were also more confident teaching sustainable food literacy skills than attitudes, values, and beliefs. Respondents who had participated in food-sustainability-focused professional development reported significantly higher self-efficacy in teaching sustainable food literacy knowledge. title: Comparing Quality in Academia Utilizing Data Envelopment Analysis: The Relationship Between Quantitative and Qualitative Indicators at Institutions of Higher Education
abstract: Israel’s system of higher education, like many national research evaluation systems worldwide, contends with a constant tension between quantitative metrics and the need to promote significant scientific excellence. This article explores the relationship between quantitative and qualitative indicators at academic institutions by utilizing the data envelopment analysis (DEA) technique. Based on analysis of 52 academic institutions (15 in Israel and 37 in other countries), we examine the performance of 47 Israel Prize laureates in the exact sciences (1978–2023), according to the criteria of Israel’s Planning and Budgeting Committee (PBC) budgeting model. The main finding reveals that only 19% of Israel Prize recipients rank in the upper quintile under the current model. Adjusting the indicators by period and discipline raises this rate to 67%, indicating a widening discrepancy between quantitative indicators and the system’s ability to detect outstanding scientific excellence. title: Somatic-First vs. Text-First Approaches: A Quasi-Experimental Study on Playwriting Pedagogy in Secondary Education
abstract: Background: Playwriting is a core module in Hong Kong’s secondary drama education curriculum; however, its effective implementation is often hindered by traditional text-first pedagogical paradigms. These conventional approaches restrict novice students’ ability to conceptualize live dramatic tension, often resulting in plays with stiff dialogue and limited stage feasibility. This study evaluated the instructional efficacy of a four-lesson somatic-first playwriting module—the somatic-generative and dual-loop reflective framework (SoDu) aligned with the LETCA rubric (Literary-language, Effective Lines, Tension, Creativity, and Stage Applicability)—compared to a conventional text-first approach. Stageability was operationalized as the extent to which written text can be effectively translated into embodied stage actions. Methods: A quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test evaluation was conducted with two Secondary 3 classes. title: Curriculum Design and Evaluation of Data Science Track for Management Students
abstract: The growing demand for data science competencies across professional fields creates a need for curricula that enable management students to develop analytical skills while navigating increasingly complex technological environments. This study examines the design and evaluation of a three-year Data Science track embedded within an undergraduate management program. The curriculum integrates statistics, programming, data management, visualization, artificial intelligence, and project-based learning within a progressively structured, multi-tool environment. A multi-cohort, multi-method design combined longitudinal academic performance data from two independent cohorts with graduates’ attitudes toward data science, career adaptability, course perceptions, and qualitative feedback. Academic performance showed cohort-specific patterns: variability decreased progressively across the three years in Cohort 1, whereas in Cohort 2 it decreased in the second year but increased in the third year. title: The Comparative Association of Personal Characteristics and Civic Activities with Socio-Economic Differences in Adolescents’ Attitudes Toward Immigrants in 21 European Educational Systems
abstract: Among many other factors, the formation of adolescents’ attitudes toward immigrants is related to multiple socio-economic, personal, and educational factors, yet little is known about their relative importance across educational systems. This study examined the relative contribution of students’ socio-economic background, personal characteristics, civic activities at school, and civic activities outside school to attitudes toward immigrants using nationally representative data from the International Civic and Citizenship Education Study 2022, including almost 70,000 participating eighth-grade students from 21 European educational systems. A series of regression models examined the extent to which different blocks of variables attenuated the association between socio-economic background and positive attitudes toward immigrants. Across the 21 educational systems, higher socio-economic background was generally associated with more positive attitudes. title: When Confidence Masks Conceptual Gaps: Examining Teachers’ Knowledge of Graphs and Procedural Approaches to Teaching
abstract: Graphs are a conceptually demanding yet foundational component of school mathematics, yet their teaching is often shaped by procedural routines that can obscure weak conceptual understanding. A persistent concern is that teachers’ confidence in teaching graphs may be mistaken for secure topic-specific knowledge, even though graph teaching requires explanation, interpretation, and responsiveness to learner thinking. This study examined how teachers’ responses to graph-related tasks reflected their confidence, conceptual understanding, and perceptions of learner difficulties in teaching Grade 8 and Grade 9 graphs. The study was guided by the Mathematical Knowledge for Teaching framework, which distinguishes between general mathematical competence and the specialized knowledge needed for teaching, including the ability to explain concepts, interpret learner thinking, and respond to misconceptions. abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence can provide individual study support, but the educational significance of its responses depends on how they are examined and used. We develop a conceptual framework comparing Individual Chatbot Interaction and Standard Classroom Interaction, then specify a Virtual Tutor with Physical Presence as a situated implementation of shared AI inquiry. The framework draws on selected scholarship concerning mediated learning, educational dialogue, self-regulation, cognitive engagement, pedagogical agents, and AI literacy. We define the unit of analysis as an interaction episode and distinguish private consultation, shared instruction, and hybrid activities through observable criteria. abstract: This study explores Foreign Language Enjoyment (FLE) among medical students learning languages with different contextual roles within the same university and taught by the same teacher under comparable instructional conditions. A total of 213 students participated, including Hungarian students learning English for medical purposes (n = 130) and international students learning Hungarian (n = 83). The Short Form of the Foreign Language Enjoyment Scale (S-FLES) was used. The ordinal confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) showed an overall adequate fit for the original three-factor S-FLES model in the full sample, providing support for this structure in the present study. abstract: Scientific argumentation is a core scientific practice recognized by multiple national science standards, yet many science teachers experience challenges integrating it into their classrooms. This systematic review examined the resources identified by research as shaping teachers’ argumentation instruction and how these resources were reported to support teachers’ classroom practice. Guided by an adapted version of the Pedagogical Design Capacity Framework, we analyzed 79 empirical studies published between 1983 and 2025. Resources were categorized as personal, instructional, or contextual, and their specific supportive aspects were grouped according to their reported contributions. Personal resources included teachers’ beliefs, knowledge of argumentation, and pedagogical content knowledge for argumentation. abstract: Graduate employability is increasingly relevant in Higher Education, yet its relationship with university administrative and support service quality remains underexplored. This study investigates whether broader configurations of administrative performance, jointly considering service effectiveness perceived and cost efficiency, are associated with differences in graduate employability. Using longitudinal data from the Italian Good Practice project (2014–2023), we analyze 45 universities across five support service areas (General Administration, Teaching and Learning Support, Campus Facilities, Research Support, and Library Services) through Latent Profile Analysis to identify distinct performance profiles and their evolution over time. abstract: Agentic translation systems, autonomous multi-agent architectures capable of planning, tool orchestration, and end-to-end translation, increasingly perform routine translation tasks that translator education programmes were historically designed to teach. Without reform, programmes risk producing graduates for occupational categories that are projected to be increasingly automated. title: Digital and AI-Supported Game-Based Interventions for Executive Function Development in Early Childhood: A Systematic Review
abstract: Executive function (EF)—working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility—underpins school readiness, academic achievement, and socio-emotional competence in early childhood (ages 3–8). Digital and AI-supported game-based interventions are a promising but underexamined modality for EF training. This review aimed to synthesize the reported effects of digital and AI-supported game-based interventions on executive function in children aged 3–8 years and the technological features linked to reported gains. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, this systematic review synthesized 19 studies from six databases (PubMed, PsycINFO, ERIC, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore) covering January 2012–March 2026, involving 1890 children aged 4–8 years across 11 countries. abstract: The consolidation of online learning in higher education raises a question teacher education can no longer defer: How is social–emotional –support created when teaching and learning are mediated by screens? This study explored how preservice teachers experienced social-emotional learning (SEL) in an online course, focusing on three dimensions: belonging, visibility, and voice. Using reflexive thematic analysis within a constructivist orientation, the study analyzed the summative written reflections, composed as letters to the lecturer, of preservice teachers (N = 27) in a year-long synchronous online course at a teacher education institution. The cohort, aged 19 to 35, was heterogeneous in life circumstances, professional experience, and learning profiles. title: Artificial Intelligence in Ecuadorian Higher Education: A PRISMA-Based Systematic Literature Review of Benefits, Challenges, and Research Gaps
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming higher education; however, evidence of its research and application in Ecuador remains fragmented. We systematically reviewed the internationally indexed literature on AI in Ecuadorian higher education. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection were searched for peer-reviewed publications from 2015 to 2025. Of the 271 unique records screened, 62 studies met the eligibility criteria; they were appraised using design-specific instruments (MMAT 2018, PROBAST) and analyzed through thematic synthesis across eight axes. The corpus concentrates on 2024–2025 (71%) and is dominated by learning analytics (16 studies) and generative AI (14 studies), followed by perception studies (10 studies). Reported benefits—early warning, efficiency, assessment support, and skill development—rest on technical performance, usability, and satisfaction rather than on measured learning or institutional gains. abstract: Bibliometric commentary increasingly frames the rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) as a paradigm shift in AI-in-education (AIED) research, yet rarely distinguishes publication growth from genuine reconfiguration of the knowledge base or of teacher–learner roles. This study maps knowledge evolution in AIED from 2015 to 2025 by integrating four analytical strands across Web of Science and Scopus: scientometric mapping (including keyword and reference bursts and co-citation analysis), structural topic modeling (STM), design-weighted coding of full texts, and triangulation across these strands. abstract: Extension lacks literature comparing standalone generative artificial intelligence (AI) with structured professional development for capacity building. We conducted a randomized 2 × 2 factorial pilot study crossing access to an evaluation certificate course with access to a custom Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT). abstract: Research on mathematics anxiety (MA) transmission has examined how teacher anxiety shapes student outcomes through instructional behavior. A more complex reality remains unaddressed. title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education—Ethical Policies Mapping
abstract: Artificial Intelligence is transforming numerous sectors, and education is no exception. The adoption of generative AI tools in higher education presents significant opportunities for enhancing teaching, learning, assessment, accessibility, and administrative processes. At the same time, their widespread use raises critical ethical concerns related to academic integrity, bias, transparency, data protection, and the possible erosion of critical thinking and creativity. In response, higher education institutions worldwide are beginning to formulate ethical guidelines to govern the use of AI by students, educators, and administrators. abstract: Traditional quantitative instruments, such as the Readiness for Interprofessional Learning Scale (RIPLS), reliably measure readiness for interprofessional education (IPE), but often miss the complex socio-cultural nuances and cognitive friction of collaborative training. This mixed-methods study aimed to capture these deeper realities by integrating open-ended qualitative questions with the validated Spanish version of RIPLS. A total of 176 undergraduate medical and nursing students participated in a high-fidelity simulation training seminar. Data was analyzed using quantitative associations alongside deductive qualitative content analysis to identify perceived strengths and weaknesses. abstract: Children increasingly encounter agriculture through mediated images and interfaces rather than sustained contact with farms. The corpus comprised audio-recorded triadic gameplay verbalizations with 14 rotating speaker-players, process notes, and written group responses. title: Developing Professional Competencies Through Authentic Formulation Troubleshooting in an Immersive Learning Environment
abstract: Undergraduate chemistry programmes increasingly need to develop professional competencies such as problem-solving, technical communication, and collaboration alongside disciplinary knowledge, yet conventional verification-based laboratory instruction rarely develops these competencies together. This study investigated whether an immersive learning environment built around authentic, iterative formulation troubleshooting was associated with differences in four professional-competency outcomes—problem-solving, technical project writing, oral presentation, and collaborative attitude—in an undergraduate Cosmetic Chemistry course. A quasi-experimental, non-equivalent comparison-group design involved 47 chemistry students in two intact classes (immersive condition, n = 25; comparison condition, n = 22). title: Object Substitution Play: A Leading Activity for Infants, Toddlers, and Preschoolers
abstract: Object substitution play can be independent of imaginary role-play and not have a storyline. In the game “hot potato” an object is tossed from one person to another, as if it was too hot to handle. Different objects can be used: a ball, a rock, a rolled-up sock, or a crunched-up piece of paper. Object substitution play can be introduced to infants at three months by caregivers moving their hand up the baby’s chest like a mouse, with a minimal narrative of “a mouse is crawling, crawling … gotcha”. Object substitution play is a precursor to pretend roleplay, and when introduced by caregivers leads to more advanced pretend play at younger ages. According to Vygotsky, this leads to the development of literacy, imagination, creativity, and abstract thinking (skills important in mathematics, science, the arts, and social studies). Introducing object substitution play with autistic children advances communication skills, and could do the same for neurotypical children. Many researchers and educators have assumed that symbolic play originates from the toddler’s solitary activities. A reimagined pedagogy would explore caregiver-initiated object substitution play beginning in early infancy.

title: Designing Verifiable Educational Simulations: Technical Verification of OpenHydroLab for Undergraduate Hydraulics and Hydrology
abstract: Interactive simulations can help students explore relationships that static figures cannot show easily. This study presents OpenHydroLab, an open-source suite of ten browser-based laboratories for undergraduate fluid mechanics, hydraulics, and hydrology. title: A Predictive Model of Bullying Perpetration Towards Students with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities in Physical Education: The Role of Motivation, Tolerance and Attitudes
abstract: Bullying towards students with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) remains a persistent problem in school contexts, yet the psychosocial mechanisms underlying bullying perpetration in inclusive settings are still insufficiently understood. Primarily grounded in Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and drawing on the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) as a complementary framework for considering attitudinal variables, this study examined a predictive model of bullying perpetration towards students with SEND in Physical Education (PE), focusing on the role of motivational and attitudinal processes. A total of 356 secondary school students (M age = 13.77; SD = 1.34) completed measures assessing perceived teaching style, basic psychological needs satisfaction, self-determined motivation, tolerance, attitudes towards disability, and bullying perpetration towards peers with disabilities. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, correlational analyses, and path analysis. title: Generative AI-Guided Versus Human-Guided Learning from Errors in Higher Education: A Comparison of Student Perceptions
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to support programming education, but its use in learning-from-errors activities has received limited research attention. This quasi-experimental study compared AI-guided and human-guided support in a structured learning-from-errors programming activity, focusing on students’ perceptions and their variability. A total of 59 college students completed the JavaScript error-detection and correction activity under AI-guided or human-guided support. Following the activity, students completed a questionnaire measuring perceived learning experience, satisfaction, general motivation, self-regulated learning (SRL), and self-efficacy. Between-group differences were examined using Mann–Whitney U tests, and differences in variability were examined using Levene’s tests. Students in the AI-guided condition reported significantly more positive learning experiences and greater satisfaction than those in the human-guided condition. abstract: Universities promote generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as a pedagogical resource while regulating it as a risk to academic integrity and fair assessment. This study examines how differentiated policy framing varies across substantive policy dimensions and national contexts, and how students interpret and navigate such guidance in practice. Using a convergent mixed-methods design with quantitative priority, we analyzed GenAI policy documents from 36 universities in Denmark, the United Kingdom, the United States, and the Netherlands, complemented by eight semi-structured interviews with graduate students at one sampled university. abstract: Preparing engineers for rapidly changing sociotechnical environments requires a clear account of the competencies that undergraduate engineering programs should foster. This study used the term future outstanding engineers to refer to engineering undergraduates being prepared for engineering excellence and examined the structure and correlates of their self-reported core competence. Cross-sectional survey data were obtained from 578 engineering undergraduates at a Chinese research university. A reflective–formative higher-order model was estimated using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM); partial least squares multigroup analysis (PLS-MGA) compared grade cohorts; and multiple linear regression examined associations with student background and educational experience. title: Bringing the 6 F-Words into Primary School: Development and Validation of the ‘I Know Myself Well’ Questionnaire
abstract: The F-Words framework introduces a holistic view of child development. This study evaluated the preliminary development and psychometric properties of the ‘I Know Myself Well’ questionnaire, a new self-report measure based on this framework. Participants included 209 primary school students in Northern Italy. Using a cross-validation framework, exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses revealed a robust two-factor structure (EFA = 90; CFA = 119): Relational Self-Awareness and Agentic Self-Projection. The scale demonstrated satisfactory fit indices and acceptable overall internal consistency. This brief tool provides a psychometrically sound, child-centered instrument to support inclusive educational planning and early career development.

title: Prompt Design as AI-Mediated Pedagogical Performance in Initial Teacher Education: A Case Study in Foreign Language Teaching Methodology
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is creating new possibilities for educational resource development, making prompt design increasingly relevant to interactions with these tools. However, little research has examined how pedagogical criteria are represented in prompts developed within initial teacher education or how prompt design can be conceptualised in relation to teachers’ professional knowledge. This study analyses 15 group-produced prompts and their documented development processes, created by students enrolled in a Bachelor’s Degree in Early Childhood Education during a Foreign Language Teaching Methodology activity involving the creation of children’s stories in English using generative artificial intelligence. An exploratory case study design was adopted, using an eight-dimension analytical rubric addressing pedagogical, linguistic, narrative, and strategic aspects of prompt design, with the corpus independently assessed by three raters. title: Partnerships for Inclusive Practices in Data-Use Teacher Communities
abstract: This article examines inclusive practices through the implementation of a data-use model in a partnership between a university and schools in a Norwegian region. Although inclusion is a key educational policy goal, research shows that its realisation in practice remains uneven. National policy documents therefore emphasise that school improvement should be developed collaboratively between universities and district leaders to build local professional capacity. In this study, 290 teachers from 18 schools participated in a questionnaire assessing the quality of support, training, leadership and their work with the data-use model, as well as perceived outcomes for teachers’ practice and students’ learning. Quantitative and qualitative analyses were conducted. Results from the factor analysis identified two components, ‘Quality’ and ‘Outcomes’, with high internal consistency. abstract: Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) aims to foster the key sustainability competencies (KSC) that enable future teachers to act as change agents. Yet little is known about how pre-service teachers interpret these competencies and their development within project- and problem-based learning settings. This study examines the perceived learning processes and self-reported competence development of pre-service primary school teachers within a four-semester, project- and problem-based ESD module. It addresses two questions: which KSC pre-service teachers perceive as further developed within the module, and what interpretations and interrelations of these competencies emerge from their reflections and self-assessments. A mixed-methods design was adopted, combining focus groups with a self-report questionnaire assessing eight KSC. abstract: Special education should empower students with disabilities as active participants in their educational experiences, yet many students, particularly those from culturally and linguistically diverse (CLD) backgrounds (a population designated CALD in some international contexts), those with more significant disabilities such as high-support-needs autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and/or intellectual/developmental disabilities (IDDs), and those experiencing socioeconomic and immigration-related challenges, continue to experience exclusion, segregation, and limited opportunities to express themselves in traditional educational settings. abstract: The increasing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has prompted growing interest in its potential in intercultural competence (IC) education. Yet research on how GenAI can support IC development remains fragmented across language education, pragmatics, pedagogy, and professional communication. This scoping review mapped research contexts, designs, theoretical foundations, and findings on GenAI-mediated IC education. abstract: Multicultural classrooms can be understood as complex adaptive learning environments in which cultural diversity, collaborative interaction, and systemic reasoning interact in non-linear ways. Although systems thinking, cooperative learning, and multicultural education have each received substantial scholarly attention, their intersections remain insufficiently synthesized. We conducted a scoping review of 120 empirical studies identified through searches of Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus, using a search window from January 1992 to June 2024. The earliest eligible empirical study was published in 2003. abstract: This document analysis reviews 12 commercial and institution-specific Individual Development Plans (IDPs) and the web content used to frame them from 22 STEM undergraduate programs across the US. Positioned as an essential career planning tool for STEM students at undergraduate and graduate levels, IDPs are intended to promote student success through self-assessment, goal setting, and planning. abstract: Teachers’ professional self-efficacy is one of the key determinants of the quality of early childhood education; however, there is little empirical evidence available on the personal psychological resources underlying its development within the Hungarian preschool education context. The aim of this cross-sectional study was to explore the relationship between emotional intelligence and professional self-efficacy, and to examine whether this relationship differs between groups representing two stages of professional socialisation. abstract: This conceptual article argues that research on reflection and reflective practice in Physical Education Teacher Education (PETE) has largely focused on content-based understandings of reflection. In response, it contends that growing attention to situated reflection can cultivate conditions for resonance, creating opportunities for a more diverse, vibrant, and responsive field of inquiry. title: Trajectories of Reading Fluency in Students with Reading Difficulties: A Systematic Review
abstract: Reading fluency is a key component of reading competence, yet its longitudinal development among students with reading difficulties remains poorly understood. This systematic review synthesized longitudinal evidence on reading fluency trajectories, associated predictors, and methodological approaches in elementary school students with reading difficulties. Following PRISMA guidelines, studies published between 2004 and 2025 were identified through searches of Scopus, ERIC, and Web of Science, complemented by citation tracking and manual screening. abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can support self-regulated learning (SRL), but its pedagogical value depends on whether interaction elicits learner cognition or substitutes for it. This study examined how students’ reported use of GenAI corresponded to an intended question-first coaching design, the perceived processes and tensions associated with SRL, and conditions relevant to potential scale. A qualitatively driven embedded case study utilized 31 reflective portfolios as the primary dataset, complemented by 53 survey responses and 68 weekly logs from 12 maximum-variation cases. Abductive, reflexive thematic analysis generated five themes. Question-led interaction appeared most useful when it prompted problem reframing, led to a bounded evidence-producing action, and preserved learner judgment through evaluation, modification, or rejection of AI suggestions. Benefits were qualified by role drift, generic interaction, cognitive substitution, uneven engagement, and continued need for human support. title: Immersive Outreach Interventions as a Tool to Foster STEM Vocation: An Observational Programme Evaluation
abstract: STEM outreach evaluations often rely on full-sample averages and general enjoyment metrics, overlooking how specific pedagogical factors relate to students without a consolidated vocation. This study evaluates the “Desayuna Ingeniería” (Breakfast Engineering) STEM outreach programme to identify intervention variables associated with perceived increases in pre-university students’ vocational interest in industrial engineering. In the retrospective survey (N = 584), 48.8% of participants reported increased interest after the visit. Focusing specifically on the target subsample of students with low or moderate prior interest, who represent the “undecided” group (n = 408), binary logistic regression models examined how active workshop participation, overall workshop satisfaction, and mentor gender configuration were associated with perceived vocational change. Active workshop participation showed a positive predictive trend that did not reach the prespecified significance threshold (p = 0.056), overall workshop satisfaction showed no statistically significant association (p = 0.697), and evidence regarding mentor gender configuration was inconclusive. title: Post-Pandemic E-Learning Practices in Higher Education: A Cross-Sectional Survey of Students and Academic Staff Across Eight Institutions in Southeastern Poland
abstract: The study examined e-learning practices reported by students and academic staff in the post-pandemic period and respondent characteristics associated with exploratory composite index scores. In October 2025, a cross-sectional survey included 1049 students and 189 academic staff members recruited through non-probability sampling at eight institutions in southeastern Poland. Each respondent-specific questionnaire included a ten-item block on e-learning practices, experiences, and barriers. Its first eight items formed separate exploratory composite indices for students and academic staff across the participating institutions. Analyses comprised descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, and two linear regression models with institution fixed effects and HC3 robust standard errors. Students most frequently endorsed items concerning online tests, synchronous classes, and improved time management. Academic staff most often reported online consultations and using communication platforms, but less frequently recording classes, creating LMS courses, or using specialized collaboration tools. title: Tools for Promoting Conceptually Productive Discussion and Argumentation in Science Education
abstract: Teachers often have difficulty facilitating whole-class science discussions that are not teacher-centric. In this study, we explore the use of a planning/reflection form (PRF) to support these discussions in three middle-school science classrooms. The PRF was based on three instructional frameworks: Ian J. Dove and E. Michael Nussbaum’s Critical Questions Model of Argument Assessment, talk moves as described in Sarah Michaels and Catherine O’Connor’s Academically Productive Talk, and an elicit-explore-consensus instructional cycle. The frameworks also provided a basis for identifying both deficiencies and successes in the teachers’ discourse practices. Data included recordings of discussions and teacher reflection meetings, analyzed for thematic discursive patterns. We found the curriculum (Amplify Science) incorporated some critical questions for evaluating arguments, but provided limited scaffolding for facilitating whole-class discussions or probing student reasoning. Teachers viewed the PRF as helping them focus on student contributions and formative assessment data. One teacher also implemented a student science seminar led by student moderators. title: Playful Writing in Arabic at Home: Mothers’ and Older Siblings’ Interactions with Preschoolers
abstract: Interactions with young children provide an important context for early literacy development. Although many of these interactions occur within the family, little is known about older siblings’ literacy interactions with younger siblings or how they compare with mothers’ interactions with the younger sibling within the same family. Using a game-based literacy activity, this study compared mother–preschooler and older sibling–preschooler interactions in terms of literacy mediation, dyadic quality, and playfulness, and examined associations among these interaction characteristics. Participants were 80 Palestinian preschoolers (ages 5–6), their mothers, and older siblings (ages 7–9). Each dyad played a structured literacy-bowling game involving constructing words using lettered pins. Mothers showed higher levels of literacy mediation (Grapho-Phonemic and spelling mediation). Regarding the dyadic aspects of the interaction, mothers displayed greater positivity, and preschoolers showed higher levels of positive engagement and dyadic reciprocity during interactions with their mothers. title: The Cost of Algorithmic Assessment: How AI Grading Undermines Academic Motivation and Amplifies AI Reliance Intentions
abstract: This research examines the psychological consequences of an AI deployment policy wherein instructors use AI to grade student work while discouraging students from using AI to produce it. Drawing on expectancy-value theory, procedural justice, social exchange, and algorithm aversion frameworks, we experimentally test a psychological model in which algorithmic (vs. human) assessment reduces perceived policy fairness and expected grading accuracy, which in turn lowers prospective students’ appraisals of the course and diminishes their intentions to exert effort. Lower willingness to exert effort, in turn, is associated with increased intentions to rely on AI for task completion against instructional policy. These effects are moderated by prior AI familiarity: individuals with less AI experience perceive algorithmic assessment as more unfair and inaccurate, amplifying negative downstream consequences. The findings contribute to the understanding of how the deployment of AI for assessment by those in authority roles shapes behavioral responses, with implications for the design of assessment policies, AI use guidelines, and instructor practice in higher education.

title: Perceived Barriers, Parental Attitudes, and Interactive Parent–Child Shared Reading: A PLS-SEM Study in Taiwan
abstract: Parent–child shared reading supports early language and literacy development, but favorable beliefs do not always translate into sustained, high-quality interaction. This cross-sectional study examined how four perceived barriers—time constraints, resource limitations, uncertainty about reading methods, and digital media interference—were associated with parents’ interactive shared-reading behavior and whether barriers were indirectly associated with behavior through parental attitudes. The analysis was informed by expectancy–value reasoning, with the barrier dimensions treated as cost-like constraints rather than as direct measures of the expectancy–value cost construct. Survey data from 309 parents and primary caregivers of preschool children in Taiwan were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with a two-stage reflective–formative higher-order construct. Parents endorsed shared reading strongly (M = 3.41 on a four-point scale) but reported more moderate interactive practice (M = 2.71). title: Enhancing Student Learning in Online STEM Labs Through Live Support: The Lab Assist Project
abstract: Remote access to laboratory equipment enables distance-learning STEM students to engage with authentic experimental activities, but some students experience barriers when using remote laboratories. This paper reports an exploratory mixed-methods study undertaken within the two-year Lab-Assist Project, which examined students’ and tutors’ perceptions of real-time or near-real-time support in remote STEM laboratory activities. Data were collected through stakeholder consultations with 13 Module Chairs, surveys of 41 students and 8 tutors, and a pilot of live-supported sessions involving two of the participating tutors within The Open University’s OpenSTEM Labs in the UK. Quantitative responses were analysed descriptively and qualitative responses thematically. Findings indicate that students valued timely and tailored support, particularly when experiencing difficulties with equipment, experimental procedures, or uncertainty about their performance. Tutor feedback highlighted challenges associated with fragmented information, preparation, and interpreting experimental tasks, providing a basis for considering the potential role of timely support in managing extraneous cognitive load.

title: Enhancing Algebra Learning: Online Tutoring as a Technological Alternative for Grade Seven Students
abstract: This study aimed to develop and evaluate the effectiveness of an online tutoring program (OTP) based on the Structure of the Observed Learning Outcome (SOLO) model and the Community of Inquiry (CoI) model for learning basic algebraic concepts step by step. The application of the OTP involved 13 mathematics teachers and 289 Grade 7 students during classroom lessons. A mixed-method approach was applied, with a quasi-experimental method used to collect quantitative data. The students’ feedback was collected through an interview survey. All the mathematics teachers were also interviewed after the implementation. The quantitative findings of the paired samples t-test showed p-values of 0.00, indicating that there was a statistically significant difference between the mean scores of algebraic expressions and linear equations after using the OTP. The results of the qualitative study showed that both student feedback and teacher provided expressive insights that extend and refine the OTP in the context of algebra teaching and learning. This study confirmed that an OTP in school settings could positively affect the teaching and learning of algebra.

title: Beyond Answer Generation: University Teachers’ Experiences with a Reflective GenAI Chatbot for Professional Learning
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used in higher education, yet limited research has examined how university teachers’ experience pedagogically designed AI systems that prioritize reflective learning over answer generation. This exploratory mixed-methods case study investigated university teachers’ experiences of a course-specific GenAI chatbot within a professional-development course at a Swedish university. All 48 course participants were invited to complete a questionnaire, of whom 21 responded and 11 reported using the course-specific chatbot; nine respondents also participated in semi-structured interviews. Questionnaire data were analyzed descriptively and interview data were analyzed using thematic analysis. The chatbot was designed to encourage dialogue, engagement with course literature, and independent thinking rather than provide summaries or ready-made answers. Participants generally found the chatbot easy to use, but perceptions of usefulness varied. title: A Triadic Programme Combining Universal Design for Learning, Multilevel Instruction and Manipulative Mathematics in Second-Grade Primary Education: A Quasi-Experimental Study of Mathematical Competence and Attitudes
abstract: Evidence on programmes that combine manipulative mathematics, Universal Design for Learning (UDL) and multilevel instruction is scarce, particularly for primary students with and without specific learning difficulties (SpLD). This study examined whether a six-session triadic programme was associated with gains in mathematical achievement and attitudes towards mathematics in second-grade students. A quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design with a non-equivalent control group was used in four schools in Castilla y León (Spain); in each school, one classroom received the programme (n = 69) and one received traditional instruction on the same content (n = 69). Mathematical fluency, calculation and mathematical competence were primary outcomes; competence sub-domains and four attitude items adapted from the TOMA-3 were secondary outcomes. title: Beyond Acceptance and Resistance: Digital Media Students’ Judgements of Generative AI Assistance and Perceived Creative Replacement
abstract: This study investigated how Digital Media students judged acceptable and problematic forms of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) involvement in creative learning. An embedded mixed-methods analysis examined 48 completed and consented baseline survey responses from an accessible population of 120 students at an Australian university. Forty-seven responses were valid for most Likert items, with qualitative content analysis of 37 benefit responses and 41 concern responses. Participants identified potential value in troubleshooting, coding support, grammar checking, information organisation, and error identification. They reported concern about AI-system training practices (93.6%), reduced employment opportunities (89.4%), the ethical acceptability of AI-supported coursework (83.0%), environmental effects (80.9%), and possible reductions in creative-skill development (76.6%). These percentages represent perceived risks, not demonstrated outcomes. title: Toward a Multidimensional Understanding of Evidence About Wellbeing in Education
abstract: Calls for evidence-based practice in wellbeing in education have expanded rapidly across research, policy and professional discourse. Yet the concept of evidence in this field often remains under-theorised and inconsistently applied. Wellbeing in education is a complex and multidisciplinary domain, informed by psychology, education, sociology, public health and philosophy and encompassing outcomes, lived experiences, relationships and contextual conditions. As a result, narrow hierarchies of evidence borrowed from medical or interventionist traditions may be insufficient for capturing the complexity of educational wellbeing. This conceptual article develops a Multidimensional Evidence Framework for understanding evidence about wellbeing in education. Drawing on a critical realist and pragmatic pluralist theoretical frame, this article proposes that robust evidence in this field includes descriptive, causal, contextual and implementation, and experiential and interpretive forms of evidence, considered through a cross-cutting equity and ethical lens. title: The Relationship Between 3D Printing Technology and STEM Education Outcomes: The Moderating Role of Institutional Infrastructure in Ethiopian Secondary Schools
abstract: The integration of 3D printing technology (3DPT) into STEM education has transformed teaching and learning through experiential and design-based approaches. However, the effectiveness of this technology is largely shaped by the institutional environment in which it is implemented. This study investigates the moderating role of institutional infrastructure in the relationship between 3DPT and STEM education outcomes (STEMO) in Ethiopian secondary schools. A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was employed, involving 368 participants from secondary schools equipped with STEM and 3D printing facilities. Data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The results indicate that the dimension of 3DPT are positively associated STEMO, with frequency of use, instructional integration, and access to digital resources showing stronger associations than availability alone. In addition, both human and digital infrastructures were positively associated with STEMO. The significant interaction effects further indicate that institutional infrastructure moderates the association between 3D printing technology and STEM education outcomes. title: Understanding Limited Participation in Collaborative Question Generation: A Mixed-Methods Study of PeerWise in Higher Education
abstract: Collaborative question-generation systems such as PeerWise can support active, collaborative, and self-regulated learning, while sustained participation remains an important implementation challenge. This study examined perceived educational value and participation descriptively in an undergraduate business information systems course. A mixed-methods case study design combined a theory-informed pre-examination questionnaire (N = 25), a post-examination questionnaire (N = 22), open-ended responses, and three focus group discussions (two with the study cohort and one with a previous cohort taught under the same design). Students generally regarded PeerWise as useful and educationally valuable, while question-generation activity remained limited and PeerWise use was concentrated close to the examination. Question creation was described as cognitively demanding and time-consuming, while other study activities often took priority. Engagement was also associated with visible peer activity, instructional guidance, and assessment relevance. The study identifies a gap between perceived educational value and sustained participation and highlights conditions associated with this gap.

title: Promoting Academic Vocabulary and Reading Comprehension Through Blended Learning: Evidence from the Golden Triangle Intervention Among Arabic-Speaking Middle School Students
abstract: Arabic-speaking adolescents face distinctive literacy challenges arising from diglossia, morphological complexity, and limited access to academic vocabulary. This quasi-experimental, non-randomized mixed-methods study examined intervention-associated changes following the Golden Triangle, a five-month blended-learning program integrating academic-vocabulary instruction, reading comprehension, digital practice, and teacher professional development. Twenty-three Arabic-medium middle schools participated (17 intervention; 6 comparison), and 731 seventh-grade students were recruited. Primary maximum-likelihood mixed-effects models included time, condition, and their interaction, with student and school random intercepts. Model-based Wald inference indicated additional gains in receptive vocabulary (B = 6.25, 95% CI [1.82, 10.67], nominal p = 0.006) and Grade-7 reading comprehension (B = 4.88, 95% CI [0.39, 9.37], nominal p = 0.033), but no statistically detectable additional gain on the Productive Academic Vocabulary Test (PAVT; B = 1.54, 95% CI [−1.92, 4.99], p = 0.384). title: Do Home Digital Resources Bridge or Widen the Achievement Gap? Evidence from PISA 2022 in Latin America and the Caribbean
abstract: Governments across Latin America and the Caribbean have invested heavily in home devices and connectivity, yet whether these resources narrow or widen socioeconomic achievement gaps remains unclear. Using Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2022 microdata from 13 education systems (N = 89,339), this study examines whether home digital resources (ICTRES) moderate the socioeconomic gradient (ESCS) in mathematics and reading, using plausible values, multiple imputation, and Fay-corrected replicate weights. The results point to amplification rather than compensation: the ESCS × ICTRES interaction was positive in mathematics (β = 2.90) and reading (β = 1.83), and the mathematics gradient rose from 9.05 points at low ICTRES to 15.57 at high ICTRES. This pattern held when ESCS was residualized on ICTRES. Adding ICTRES reduced the baseline mathematics gradient (19.46 points) by 37.0%, but this attenuation largely reflects variance shared by two partially overlapping indices, so the accompanying decomposition is reported only descriptively. title: Identifying Barriers to Using Generative AI in Education Through AI-Assisted Literature Mining of arXiv Articles
abstract: This study presents an exploratory, generative AI (GenAI)-assisted full-text analysis of barriers to using GenAI in education within an arXiv corpus. A total of 19,756 records were retrieved using a keyword search and then screened for relevance using three large language models (LLMs), GPT-4o mini, Gemini 2.0 flash-lite, and Llama3-70B (Groq), through a voting mechanism. This yielded a corpus of 1998 education-relevant full-text articles. Using GPT-4o, learning and teaching scenarios (LTSs) were extracted using a structured 6As framework (Actor, Activity, AI Role, AI Interface, Assessment, Achievement) developed for this study. Barrier themes were derived separately by clustering a total of 4729 barrier descriptions, embedded using OpenAI’s embedding model. The descriptive results indicate: (i) STEM (science, technology, engineering, and mathematics) vs. non-STEM distributions of GenAI use cases are broadly comparable; (ii) approximately 75% of reported GenAI intervention outcomes were classified as non-negative across the different disciplines; and (iii) reported barriers show different descriptive patterns between STEM and non-STEM disciplines. title: Continuity and Developmental Differentiation of Educational Beliefs Across the 0–6 Developmental Continuum: Parents’ and ECEC Professionals’ Representations of Early Childhood Education
abstract: Continuity is a fundamental principle of integrated Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) systems, yet little is known about how adults’ educational beliefs vary across developmental references. The study examined developmental differentiation in educational beliefs when adults refer to children aged 0–3 versus 3–6 years and whether this differentiation varied across parents and ECEC professionals. Participants were 697 parents, 243 nursery educators, and 160 preschool teachers from ECEC services in Northern Italy. They completed two parallel versions of the Pre-K Survey of Beliefs and the Socialization Goals Scale. The two parallel Educational Beliefs forms showed metric and partial scalar invariance across developmental references. A mixed-design ANOVA showed less child-initiated beliefs for the 3–6 reference and a significant developmental-reference × respondent-role interaction of modest magnitude. title: Perceptions of a New Boundary-Crossing Professional in Early Childhood Education and Care
abstract: There is a growing trend in which new professional roles complement traditional ones to bridge education, childcare, and social care. In the Netherlands, this is reflected in the introduction of the Pedagogical Educational Professional (PEP) as a boundary-crossing professional in pre-service education. In a mixed-methods study with a vignette-based survey (N = 422), followed by three focus group discussions (N = 14), we explored how staff from childcare and primary education, and Integrated Child Centers perceive this new professional. Findings show that perceptions of the PEP are highly context-dependent. Primary education professionals mainly recognized and valued the PEP as a pragmatic generalist providing flexible support, whereas childcare and integrated childcare professionals more strongly recognized boundary-crossing roles related to collaboration, continuity, innovation, and inclusion. These differences reflect challenges in developing knowledgeability through engagement, imagination, and alignment. title: Is Online Learning Really Ready for International Students? Acceptance, Participation, and Cultural Responsiveness in U.S. Higher Education
abstract: Online learning is now widespread in the United States (U.S.) higher education, but its readiness for international students has not been fully explored outside the context of technical access. This mixed-methods study examined acceptance, participation, and cultural responsiveness among international students at a large public research university in the southeastern United States. Data included 105 surveys and 11 semi-structured interviews. Quantitative survey data were analyzed statistically; open-ended survey responses were analyzed using qualitative content analysis; and interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis. Students generally viewed online learning as accessible, manageable, useful, and worth continuing, while ratings of community and interaction were less positive, particularly among students with only asynchronous course experience. title: Development of a Machine-Learning-Based Predictive Model for Burnout Among Senior High School Teachers
abstract: Teacher burnout is a persistent problem characterized by psychological exhaustion and occupational stress, posing serious constraints on teachers’ professional development, the improvement of teaching quality, and the stable functioning of the educational ecosystem. Conventional questionnaire-based surveys, which dominate teacher burnout research, primarily assess prevalence and bivariate correlations, often at the expense of predictive precision. Such approaches often have limited predictive accuracy and generalizability, making it difficult to identify teachers at risk of burnout with precision. To develop a more effective predictive model for burnout among senior high school teachers and clarify its key underlying mechanisms, this study recruited 2441 in-service teachers from 42 senior high schools in Guangdong Province and the Macao Special Administrative Region of China. The performance of logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost was compared to identify the optimal predictive framework. title: ADHD and Autism in Online Higher Education: A Scoping Review and Thematic Synthesis of Reported Challenges
abstract: Studies involving students with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and/or autism have reported a range of challenges in higher education that may affect academic success and retention. Yet, most existing reviews focus on in-person settings at primary or secondary levels. Few studies address online higher education specifically for students with ADHD and/or autism, leaving a critical evidence gap. This scoping review and thematic synthesis, therefore, examines challenges reported in studies involving students with ADHD and/or autism in online higher education. Following the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology, the Population-Concept-Context (PCC) framework and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a focused database search, supplemented by backward and forward citation searching, resulted in the inclusion of 39 studies. The findings were synthesised thematically. title: The Digital Divide in Higher Education: A Systematic Review with the Three-Level Digital Divide Model and PEOPLE Framework
abstract: We systematically reviewed 36 peer-reviewed studies from 3829 articles across 25 countries between 2018 and 2023. Our PEOPLE framework—psychological determinants of learning, educational opportunities, educational processes, learning outcomes, and educational effectiveness—captures the impact of the digital divide on the university learning experience from a multidimensional perspective. Findings show the divide persists in both developing (56%) and developed (44%) countries, with research emphasizing access over skills or benefits. title: Fostering Attitudes and Communicative Self-Efficacy Through Structured Group Discussions on Environmental Socioscientific Issues
abstract: Group discussions enable argumentative development and are considered as a core strategy for addressing socioscientific issues (SSIs). Yet, in SSIs, students often struggle to navigate the decision-making process. This has increased interest in scaffolds that make both the process and the factual and normative complexity manageable. Although effects on the discussion process have been researched, little is known about whether structured discussion influences dispositions for future engagement, including discussion-related attitudes, communicative self-efficacy, and environmental attitudes. Therefore, this study investigated group discussions on three SSIs with 56 secondary students from four 7th- and 8th-grade classes at two German schools. In the experimental condition, discussions were supported by a scaffold called Target-Mat, which visually structured the discussion steps; the control condition used a familiar pro–con table.
